sens: one who commits sin, who transgresses God's law
guilty before God, deserving condemnation
exposed to divine judgment
H2400.detail:
1. The sinner is one who commits sin, that is, who transgresses God's commandments. The text contrasts him with the righteous: while the righteous acts according to God's will, the sinner violates it. This is clearly seen in the Psalms, where the sinner "transgresses" God's ways and opposes His order (Psalms 51:15).

2. The sinner is guilty and deserves condemnation. He is not merely someone who has made a mistake; he is someone who, through his sin, has placed himself in a position to be judged and punished. The inhabitants of Sodom are called "great sinners": they are not just at fault, they are guilty before the Lord (Genesis 13:13).

3. The sinner is exposed to divine judgment and destruction. The Psalms and the prophets show this: the sinner "will not stand in the day of judgment," he will be "destroyed" along with the wicked (Psalms 1:5, Isaiah 13:9). This is a condition of permanent peril.
H2400.origine: The Hebrew word chattat comes from a root that literally means "to miss the mark, to go astray." The sinner is one who deviates from the path that God has laid out. The same root produces the word "sin" (het), of which the sinner is the active subject. In Greek, translators often rendered this term as "hamartôlos," which retains the same image of one who "misses" or "goes astray."
H2400.emploi: This word appears 19 times in the Old Testament. It is concentrated in the Psalms and Proverbs, which constantly contrast the sinner and the righteous: the sinner experiences misfortune (Proverbs 13:21), while the righteous receive blessings. In the prophets (Isaiah, Amos), the sinner is threatened with destruction on the day of God's judgment. The term also appears in sacred history: Sodom is a kingdom of sinners (Genesis 13:13), and Saul is commanded to wage war against the Amalekites, sinners who have deserved their destruction (1 Samuel 15:18). The word always describes a moral reality and a destiny: one who sins incurs judgment.
H2400.portee: This word reminds the reader of the serious reality of sin: it is not a mere mistake, but a transgression before God that exposes one to judgment. At the same time, God calls sinners to return and teaches them (Psalms 51:15), which opens a path of repentance. For the Christian, this word is an invitation to face sin and seek grace from God.

sens: Act or state of moral guilt before God
Voluntary or involuntary transgression of divine will
Ritual offering to atone for sin and restore relationship with God
H2401.detail:
1. Sin is primarily a fault committed against God, a disobedience to His commandments. This is what Abimelech reproaches Abraham: "What have you done to us? […] You have committed acts against me that ought not to be done" (Genesis 20:9). Sin can be grave and collective, as in Israel's case with the golden calf: "You have committed a great sin" (Exodus 32:30).
2. Sin also refers to the state of guilt that results from it, a moral stain that separates the sinner from God and demands forgiveness. This is why Psalm 32:1 sings: "Blessed is he whose […] sin is forgiven!" — forgiveness erases this guilt.
3. In a cultic context, the word can refer to the sacrificial offering intended to atone for sin: one speaks of "a sacrifice for sin" or "an expiatory offering" to restore the broken relationship with God.
H2401.origine: The Hebrew word חֲטָאָה comes from the root חטא, which means "to miss the mark," "to miss the target" — like an arrow that does not hit its target. This image evokes the idea that sin is a deviation from God's will, a departure from the right path. The same root produces the verb "to sin" and the noun "sinner." In Aramaic, the parallel form is חַטָּאָה.
H2401.emploi: This word appears 8 times in the provided Hebrew texts. It is used to describe human sin, from the most concrete (Abraham's unfaithfulness to Abimelech, Genesis 20:9) to the most serious (Israel's idolatry with the golden calf, Exodus 32:21, 30, 31). Two passages from the Psalms (32:1 and 40:7) use it in the sense of spiritual guilt that demands divine forgiveness. Moses constantly uses the word to call the people to account for their transgression and the possibility of forgiveness. Sin is always presented as a serious rupture of the relationship with God, not a mere mistake.
H2401.portee: Understanding sin in biblical Hebrew as a "missing of the target" helps the believer see that sin is never neutral: it is a deviation from God's good will, which harms our relationship with Him. This explains why God gives Israel a sacrificial system: it is not about magic, but a way for the sinner to acknowledge his fault, confess it, and be restored. The New Testament will interpret Jesus as the unique Sacrifice that erases all sins (Hebrews 10:12).

sens: Animal offering presented to God to obtain forgiveness for a sin or impurity
Victim offered at the temple to turn away divine anger and restore communion with God
By extension, any action or attitude intended to erase a fault
H2402.detail:
1. The expiatory sacrifice is an animal (bull, ram, lamb, or goat) that was slaughtered at the temple according to the rules of the Law of Moses. In Ezra 6:17, during the dedication of the temple rebuilt after the exile, twelve "expiatory" goats were offered — one for each tribe of Israel — so that God would forgive the sins of the people. It was a concrete, ritualized act that acknowledged the wrong done and implored divine forgiveness.
2. Spiritually, this sacrifice represents the means established by God Himself to erase sin and restore the relationship between the guilty man and the offended God. The animal symbolically took upon itself the guilt, and its shed blood "ran" for the life of the sinner (Leviticus 17:11). It was the visible expression of divine grace that accepts a substitute for the guilty.
H2402.origine: The Hebrew word חַטָּאָה (chat.ta.ah) comes from the root חטא (ḥ-t-') which fundamentally means "to miss the target" or "to miss the goal." This is why it has been translated as "sin": sin is a deviation, a departure from God's will and justice. The Aramaic word חֲטָאָה (used here in the book of Ezra, which is partially written in Aramaic) retains the same root and meaning. The "expiatory sacrifice" is therefore the offering that responds to sin, that erases it, that "brings the aim back on target."
H2402.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezra 6:17, in the Aramaic form. It is found in the account of the reconstruction of the temple in Jerusalem after the return from exile (circa 515 B.C.). The Persian authorities had ordered a major offering: one hundred bulls, two hundred rams, four hundred lambs, and twelve "expiatory" goats. The number twelve was symbolic — one victim per tribe, so that all Israel would be purified and the temple would regain its holiness. This context shows the crucial importance of the sacrifice to restore the bond between the people and their God after the rupture of exile.
H2402.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that God has provided a concrete means to deal with sin: the sacrifice. In the Old Testament, these offerings taught that one cannot ignore the evil one commits, and that a victim, a price, is needed for reconciliation. For the Christian, this ancient practice finds its fulfillment in Jesus Christ, the "Lamb of God" (John 1:29), who offers once and for all the perfect and definitive sacrifice. Understanding what an expiatory sacrifice meant for an Israelite allows one to grasp the greatness of what Christ has accomplished.

sens: Act of disobedience to God, transgression of His law
Guilty action or inherently bad thing
Resulting guilt that exposes to divine punishment
H2403A.detail:
1. Sin is primarily an act: one who disobeys God, who transgresses His commandments. In Exodus 34:7, God lists three forms of evil — iniquity, rebellion, and sin — as ways of turning away from Him. It is a concrete action, a gesture or word that violates divine will.
2. Sin can also refer to the bad thing itself, the guilty act considered as an object. In Isaiah 5:18, the prophet speaks of those who "draw sin as with the cords of a cart": he imagines it as something that is dragged along, accumulated voluntarily, almost like a spoil that one gathers.
3. Finally, sin carries with it guilt and condemnation: this is why Exodus 34:7 specifies that God "will not hold the guilty as innocent" and "punishes iniquity." Sin creates a debt to God and exposes the one who commits it to judgment.
H2403A.origine: The Hebrew word חַטָּאָה (chat.ta.ah) comes from the root חטא (het), which literally means "to miss the mark" or "to stray from the path." This foundational image — that of the archer who misses his target — has been enriched to designate any act that deviates from divine will. The word is related to other Hebrew terms for moral evil (עָוֹן avon, iniquity; פֶּשַׁע pesha, rebellion), but retains this specific connotation of failure or deviation.
H2403A.emploi: The word appears twice in the provided usages, but its use in the Bible is constant and central. In Exodus 34:7, it appears in the solemn description of God's character after the golden calf: God forgives sin, but does not ignore it and punishes its consequences. In Isaiah 5:18, the prophet denounces those who "draw sin" voluntarily, as if they are accumulating weight towards their ruin. The Old Testament context shows that sin is never a mere slip-up: it is a serious moral reality that separates man from God and requires forgiveness and restitution.
H2403A.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that sin is not a trivial weakness, but a rupture with God — a conscious or unconscious deviation from His will. Exodus 34:7 reveals the tension in God's heart: He hates sin and punishes its fruits, but remains merciful to those who turn away from evil. Isaiah 5:18 warns that those who persist in sin load themselves with a weight that will lead to their destruction — an image that every believer can relate to in their own struggle against evil.

sens: Act or word that transgresses divine law, disobedience to God
State of guilt or guilty condition before God
Punishment or consequence of sin
Sacrifice or offering to obtain forgiveness of sins
H2403B.detail:
1. Sin is primarily a concrete act: doing evil, acting against God's will. In Genesis 4:7, sin lies at the door like an animal ready to pounce on Cain — it is a power that seeks to dominate us, but can be repelled through vigilance. This is what one commits when one disobeys (1 Kings 15:3: the king gave in to the sins of his father).
2. Sin also describes the state of guilt that results: one becomes guilty before God. This is why one can ask for forgiveness "for his sin" (Jeremiah 31:34: God will forgive their sin and will remember it no more).
3. The word can designate the punishment or consequence of sin: suffering the blows for one's sins (Leviticus 26:24: God will strike you seven times more for your sins).
4. In the laws of Leviticus, "sin" also becomes the name of the offering presented to God for purification (Leviticus 4:3, 4:14, 4:26 speak of the sin offering, the ritual that removes guilt).
H2403B.origine: The Hebrew word חַטָּאת comes from the root חטא, which means "to miss the mark," "to do wrong." It is the image of the archer who misses his target: sin is missing the path that God has laid out for us. The same root also produces the verb "to sin" and the noun "sinner" (one who misses the mark). In Greek, the New Testament translates this word as ἁμαρτία (hamartía), which carries the same image of missing the mark, of deviation.
H2403B.emploi: The word appears about 160 times in the Old Testament, especially in the Torah and the history of Israel. In Genesis and Exodus, it designates the act of disobedience (Genesis 4:7, Exodus 32:30). In Leviticus and Numbers, it takes on a strongly ritual meaning: it is the name of the sacrifice offered to reconcile with God (Leviticus 4 in detail). In the historical books (Kings, Chronicles), the sins of the kings are enumerated — always in the plural — to show how each accumulates guilt (1 Kings 15:3). The prophets use it to call for repentance (Jeremiah 31:34: the forgiveness of sin is the promise of the new covenant). The meaning oscillates between the act, the guilt, and the rite that purifies it.
H2403B.portee: This word reminds us that sin is never neutral: it is a reality that separates us from God and has consequences. But the Bible also speaks of it as something that can be fought against (Genesis 4:7) and especially that can be forgiven through sacrifice, and then by grace. For the Christian, this word anchors the understanding of salvation: we have all sinned, but Christ offers Himself as the unique sacrifice that takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29).

sens: The moral or religious failure towards God
The act of offering an animal at the temple to erase sin and reconcile the sinner with God
The animal offered as a sacrifice for this purpose
The state of guilt or defilement incurred by sin
The ritual purification of legal impurity
The means to repair a fault and restore peace with God
H2403H.detail:
1. The failure towards God: this is sin itself, that is to say, the moral or religious evil committed against divine law (Leviticus 4:3 speaks of the "sin of the priest").
2. The sacrifice offered: this is an animal — bull, ram, goat, or pigeon according to the rank of the sinner — that was brought to the sanctuary for the priest to offer, thus erasing the sin before God (Exodus 29:14 describes the bull of the sin offering).
3. The animal itself: the sin offering was the animal that bore, in a sense, the sin of the people or the penitent (Leviticus 10:19 mentions the sin offering that Aaron refused to eat).
4. The guilt incurred: this is the state of one who has sinned, the moral defilement that separates him from God until atonement is made (Numbers 15:24 speaks of the unintentional sin of the assembly).
5. The legal purification: this sacrifice also removed the ritual impurity of one who had touched a corpse or incurred ceremonial defilement (Numbers 6:11 prescribes a sin offering for the Nazarite after a death).
6. The restoration of the covenant: the atonement aimed to reconcile the sinner with God, allowing him to approach the purified sanctuary and restored in divine communion.
H2403H.origine: The Hebrew word חַטָּאת (chat.tat) comes from the root חטא (ḥṭʾ) which means "to miss the mark, to sin," a common image in Hebrew for sin. The same root designates both the sin itself and the sacrifice intended to erase it: to offer an atonement literally means "to repair the failure." This term entered the cultic system of Israel as one of the four major sacrifices of the Temple, where it held a central place in reconciliation with God.
H2403H.emploi: The word appears 110 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in the Pentateuch and especially in Leviticus and Numbers (Exodus 29-30, Leviticus 4-16, Numbers 6-28). The context is always that of the Temple: sin offerings had to be offered after a voluntary or involuntary sin (Leviticus 4-5), during ceremonial purifications (Leviticus 12, 14, 15), on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16), and during prescribed offerings for special vows such as the Nazarite vow (Numbers 6:11). The expressions vary: "sin offering," "sin bearer," "offering of atonement." The word designates both the sin that requires repair and the sacrifice that obtains it, for by offering the animal, the sinner acknowledges his sin and accepts his atonement. No profane or purely metaphorical usage appears: the term remains anchored in the institutional worship of the Temple.
H2403H.portee: Atonement reveals that sin has a price, creating a concrete rupture between the sinner and God that can only be repaired by an act of restitution. It also shows that God has instituted a path of reconciliation accessible to all, rich or poor: even the most destitute could offer two doves or flour (Leviticus 5:7, 11). For the Christian, this system of repeated sacrifices points to the uniqueness of the sacrifice of Jesus Christ once for all, which accomplishes what all the sacrifices of the Old Testament foreshadowed.

sens: Act of sinning, transgression of divine law
State of guilt resulting from it
Punishment inflicted for sin
Purification offering presented at the temple to obtain forgiveness
H2403I.detail:
1. Sin is the act of disobeying God, crossing the boundary He has set. It is the guilty action itself, the gesture that offends the Lord.
2. After committing sin, one remains guilty until forgiven: this is the state of moral defilement that one bears. Lamentations 4:6 speaks of this by comparing the punishment of Jerusalem to that of Sodom.
3. Punishment is the consequence, the penalty that God inflicts for the sin committed. Zechariah 14:19 announces the punishment that Egypt and the nations will suffer for refusing to worship the Lord.
4. To be purified, Israel must present a special offering to God: this is the sin offering (literally an offering for sin). Numbers 8:7 speaks of the purifying sprinkling water for the Levites to cleanse them of their defilement.
H2403I.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to miss the target" or "to fail," hence the idea of deviation, of fault. It refers to the image of an arrow that does not hit its mark: missing the path that God has laid out. In biblical Hebrew, the same word designates both sin (the action), guilt (the state), punishment (the consequence), and offering (the remedy). This semantic richness reflects Israel's view: sin automatically brings defilement and punishment, from which only sacrifice can liberate.
H2403I.emploi: This word appears primarily in the Law and in the prophets. It is very frequent in the sacrificial system of Leviticus and Numbers, where the "sin offering" (literally offering of punishment) is one of the five prescribed sacrifices. Here, Numbers 8:7 uses it for the purifying sprinkling water for the Levites. In the prophets, the meaning shifts towards divine punishment: Lamentations 4:6 and Zechariah 14:19 speak of the punishment that God imposes on the nations that reject Him or rebel against Him. The context thus shows how the same word can designate the religious remedy (the offering) or the sanction (the divine punishment).
H2403I.portee: This word reminds the believer that sin is not a mere moral error: it is a transgression of God's will that defiles and leads to punishment. But it also shows that there is a way of purification through sacrifice, a possible reconciliation. For the Christian, it sheds light on the role of Christ's sacrifice: Jesus became our definitive offering, the one that purifies us from all guilt and spares us from final punishment.

sens: To fell or saw wood with an axe or saw
To split or divide wood into pieces
To shape or carve wood
To engage in the work of a woodcutter or carpenter
H2404.detail: 1. The primary meaning is very concrete: it is to fell a tree or saw it to reduce it to pieces. Thus in Deuteronomy 19:5, a man "cuts wood" in the forest with his axe: it is an ordinary manual labor, but dangerous — the iron can slip from the handle and cause injury. 2. The word also designates the regular work of the woodcutter or carpenter who divides wood into usable pieces. The Gibeonites are condemned to "cut wood" for the assembly of Israel (Joshua 9:21, 9:23, 9:27): it is a servitude, a hard and endless task. 3. The word can also evoke the sculpture or shaping of wood into crafted forms, although this meaning is less frequent in the provided usages. 4. By extension, "cutting wood" becomes a trade or function: one speaks of the one "who cuts your wood" (Deuteronomy 29:11) to designate the woodcutter or servant assigned to this task.
H2404.origine: The Hebrew verb חָטַב (chatav) comes from a root that expresses the idea of striking, dividing, cutting. It is related to tools that strike: the axe, the saw. The word is akin to other Hebrew terms of the same family that all evoke the physical work of wood — split, hollowed, transformed. In the Greek of the Old Testament, this verb is often rendered by ἐκκόπτω (ekkoptô), "to cut out," or σχίζω (schizô), "to split." The basic image is therefore that of a sharp blow, of wood that divides under the shock of the tool.
H2404.emploi: This verb appears nine times in the Bible, mostly in the historical and legislative accounts of the Old Testament. In Deuteronomy (19:5 and 29:11), it describes the ordinary work of the woodcutter: felling a tree in the forest. In the account of Joshua (9:21, 9:23, 9:27), it becomes the expression of a servitude imposed on the Gibeonites: they must cut wood for the sanctuary, an endless task. In 2 Chronicles 2:10, the king seeks workers "who will cut and fell the trees" for the construction of the Temple: it is the specialized work of the carpenter. The context thus varies from daily work to servile labor, passing through skilled trades.
H2404.portee: This word reminds Christians of the dignity of all honest work, even manual and humble — felling wood was a respectable job in Israel, which the king himself needed for his projects. It also evokes the cost of labor: the workers who "cut the wood" must be fed and paid (2 Chronicles 2:10). Finally, it confronts us with the reality of servitude and forced labor — a reminder that sin and disobedience can reduce us to endless servitude, an image of the human condition without Christ.

sens: Woven fabric used to cover a bed or adorn a room
Dark or shaded fabric
H2405.detail:
1. A carpet is a fabric, a piece of cloth shaped and decorated, used to cover a bed or to beautify a space. The word evokes something precious and crafted. In Proverbs 7:16, a woman speaks of her bed adorned with carpets imported from Egypt, suggesting a fine and costly fabric.
2. The word also emphasizes the nature of this fabric: it consists of dark or shaded fabrics, which made it a valuable object and a sign of wealth or elegance in the ancient world.
H2405.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning to cut or slice, as the carpet was a cut fabric, that is, woven and crafted with care. The form of the word suggests an object of value, a noble material transformed by artisanal work.
H2405.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Proverbs 7:16. There it designates the linen coverings from Egypt with which the adulterous woman adorns her bed to seduce the young man. The context shows that these carpets represent luxury, voluptuous comfort, and wealth, elements of the seduction trap.
H2405.portee: This word reminds us that material luxury and tempting comfort can hide a spiritual trap. The beautiful carpets on the bed in this passage are not a problem in themselves, but they symbolize how sin wraps its prey in attractive and pleasant appearances. It is a lesson on vigilance against the seductions of the world.

sens: The plant that produces grains for human food
The grains themselves, harvested and ready to be milled
The flour or dough obtained after milling
The staple food that sustains
H2406.detail: 1. Wheat is primarily the plant itself, cultivated in the fields of the Levant: we speak of "the wheat harvest" (1 Samuel 12:17), a crucial time when farmers harvest the ripe ears. 2. The word also designates the harvested grains, stored or offered as tribute: Jeremiah mentions provisions of "wheat" hidden in the fields (Jeremiah 41:8). 3. It can evoke wheat transformed into flour or dough prepared for sacrifice: Exodus 29:2 speaks of "unleavened bread kneaded with oil," made from this flour. 4. Finally, wheat symbolizes abundance and divine blessing: the psalmist sings that God feeds His people with the "best wheat" (Psalms 81:17), an image of generosity and sustenance.
H2406.origine: The Hebrew word חִטָּה (chittah) comes from a root that expresses the idea of grains or small elements. In Aramaic, a similar form חִנְטָה (chintah) is found. Wheat was the major cereal of the ancient Mediterranean world, the basis of sustenance in Israel as well as in Egypt and Mesopotamia. This is why this word appears very early in the Bible and in documents of the time.
H2406.emploi: The word appears about 30 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in historical accounts and legal texts. It is encountered during harvests (Genesis 30:14, 1 Samuel 12:17), in royal tributes and taxes (1 Kings 5:11, 2 Chronicles 2:10, 2 Chronicles 27:5), and in sacrificial prescriptions (Exodus 29:2, Ezekiel 4:9). Wheat is also a blessing promised by God (Deuteronomy 8:8, where it is among the seven characteristic species of Canaan) and a staple food in times of distress. Its absence or destruction are signs of divine judgment (Joel 1:11).
H2406.portee: Wheat reminds the people of God of their dependence on His providence: one must plow, sow, and harvest, but it is God who gives the growth. Eating the "best wheat" is not just a physical act, but an expression of divine tenderness towards His people. This word invites the believer to recognize in daily bread, and especially in the bread of sacrifice, the beneficial work of the Lord.

sens: Descendant of David and son of Schemaiah, according to 1 Chronicles 3:22
H2407G.detail: Hattusch is a man of the people of Judah mentioned in the genealogy of David in 1 Chronicles 3:22. He was the son of Schemaiah and the brother of other children: Jigueal, Bariach, Neariah, and Schaphath. He represents a direct lineage in the royal house of Judah, situated four or five generations after Zerubbabel, the leader who brought the exiles back from Babylon.
H2407G.origine: The name Hattusch means "assembled" in Hebrew, evoking the idea of gathering or meeting. It belongs to a family of names of royal descent, carefully inscribed in the genealogical records of Israel to preserve the memory of the Davidic lineage after the exile.
H2407G.emploi: Hattusch appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 3:22, in the genealogical list of David's descendants. It is a name among the genealogies of the Chronicler, who is interested in the continuity of the royal house after the Babylonian exile. This mention places Hattusch in the official history of the people of Judah and its dynasty.

sens: man of the royal family of David returned from exile
descendant of Shecaniah who accompanied Ezra
H2407H.detail:
1. Hatthusch is a man of some importance at the time of the return from exile, belonging to the royal lineage of David: he is mentioned as being from "David" and "Shecaniah" (Ezra 8:2). His name appears among those who returned from Babylon with Ezra, indicating that he was a recognized figure of the restored people.
2. His precise role in the return and reconstruction is not detailed in the Bible: it is only known that he accompanied the movement of restoration of the Jewish people, likely in the generations that followed the exile.
H2407H.origine: The name Hatthusch means "gathered" in Hebrew: an image of assembly, perhaps to remind of the gathering of the dispersed people at the time of the return from captivity. Although the biblical text is lacking in details about the exact origins, the name suggests a figure linked to community restoration.
H2407H.emploi: Hatthusch appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 8:2. This passage lists the family leaders who returned from exile with Ezra, and Hatthusch is cited as a descendant of David and Shecaniah, which gives him a prominent place among the repatriates. His unique appearance shows that he was a figure of the return, undoubtedly of prestige due to his connection with the royal house.

sens: Man who participated in the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem
H2407I.detail: Hattusch is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time of the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem under the leadership of Nehemiah. He is presented as the son of Hashabnia and worked on the repair of the wall, fulfilling his part in this great collective project (Nehemiah 3:10).
H2407I.origine: The name Hattusch means "gathered" in Hebrew. It evokes the idea of assembly, which is fitting for a man remembered precisely because he joined the community for a common work: the restoration of the holy city after the exile.
H2407I.emploi: Hattusch is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 3:10. In this passage, Nehemiah lists the various groups and individuals who participated in the repair of the walls of Jerusalem after the return from exile. Hattusch is among the workers who "worked" on this reconstruction, each taking charge of a particular section of the wall. This detailed enumeration shows the involvement of the entire community, from the high priest to the ordinary inhabitants.
H2407I.portee: Hattusch embodies the role of the ordinary faithful who engage in the community work of spiritual and material reconstruction after a period of ruin. His inclusion in the list of builders reminds that every person, even humble and little mentioned, has their place and importance in God's project for His restored people.

sens: Descendant de David revenu de l'exil
Chef lévite du temps de Néhémie
H2407J.detail: 1. Hattusch is a man of the lineage of David who lived at the time of the return from exile to Jerusalem. He is mentioned as one of the signers of the covenant that the people made under the leadership of Nehemiah (Nehemiah 10:4), which shows his status as a notable or leader among those who returned from captivity. 2. Hattusch is also the name of a priest or a Levite leader who returned with the priests at the time of Nehemiah (Nehemiah 12:2). He is among those who participated in the restoration of Jerusalem and the reorganization of temple worship.
H2407J.origine: The name Hattusch means "gathered" or "assembled." It is borne by men of the people of God who participated in the return from the Babylonian exile, a pivotal period when the Israelites regrouped to rebuild their nation and their faith around God.
H2407J.emploi: Hattusch appears twice in the book of Nehemiah, written after the return from Babylon. In Nehemiah 10:4, he is among the signers of the renewed covenant between God and His people under Nehemiah, indicating that he was a man of religious and political importance. In Nehemiah 12:2, he is cited among the priests and Levite leaders who returned with the exiles. These two mentions suggest that it is the same person or closely related figures, active in the reconstruction of Jerusalem after the exile.

sens: Violation of God's law or will
Moral and religious transgression or infraction
Resulting guilt
H2408.detail:
1. Sin is a violation of God's law or will — an action or attitude that opposes what God requires. In Daniel 4:27, King Nebuchadnezzar is urged to "put an end to [his] sins by practicing righteousness," which shows that sin manifests concretely through unjust acts and that one can turn away from it.
2. It is a moral and religious transgression, a voluntary or involuntary disobedience toward God. It concerns not only visible acts but also the intentions and behaviors of the heart.
3. Sin carries with it guilt and consequences — a debt to God that requires restitution or forgiveness to be erased.
H2408.origine: This Aramaic word directly derives from the Hebrew חֵטְא (chéta), a very frequent word in the Old Testament. Both come from a root meaning "to miss the target" or "to stray," a strong image: sin is like a shot that deviates from its aim, a deviation from the straight path that God lays out. The same root produces words for "error" and "failure."
H2408.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 4:27, in the context of the late Aramaic of the book of Daniel. The prophet Daniel speaks to King Nebuchadnezzar and encourages him to "put an end to your sins by practicing righteousness." Here, sin is linked to social injustice — the absence of compassion toward the unfortunate — and the passage suggests that by changing his behavior, the king could prolong his happiness. It is an invitation to practical repentance and a morally just life.
H2408.portee: This word reminds us that sin is not a fatality: it can be abandoned and stopped. The text encourages the repentant to act concretely — to practice righteousness, to show compassion — for God's love offers a way out and the possibility of a restored life. It is a call to change, filled with hope.

sens: Man of the tribe of Levi, ancestor of a family of temple porters
H2410.detail: Hathitha is the name of a Levitical ancestor whose descendants served as porters or gatekeepers of the temple. His name literally means "the one who explores" or "who scrutinizes," an evocative image for someone charged with monitoring and verifying who enters and exits. After the Babylonian exile, his family returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel and was among the 139 porters of the temple (Ezra 2:42). This genealogy is reaffirmed a few decades later at the time of Nehemiah, with a similar number of 138 porters (Nehemiah 7:45), attesting to the continuity and importance of this function in the service of the restored worship.
H2410.origine: The Hebrew name חֲטִיטָא comes from a root expressing the idea of scrutinizing or exploring — a natural image for a guardian who must examine and control the comings and goings. It is an essential function in the structure of Jewish worship: the temple porters were not mere servants, but Levites, members of the sacred tribe dedicated to divine service.
H2410.emploi: Hathitha appears only twice in the Bible, both times at the time of the return from exile (circa 538 B.C.). Ezra 2:42 lists his family among the 139 porters who returned with Zerubbabel, and Nehemiah 7:45 repeats the same genealogy with a slightly revised number (138). These two passages are administrative or genealogical lists of the restored people, establishing the identity and status of the Levitical families. The repeated mention emphasizes that the temple worship and its essential functions were properly restored after the ruin of the exile.
H2410.portee: The presence of Hathitha and his family in these lists reminds the people of God that the restoration of the temple did not happen by chance: the families that served there before the exile were able to resume their service, which testifies to God's faithfulness to His people and the continuity of His worship. It is an assurance that even after captivity and destruction, the Lord gathers His people and restores what was destroyed.

sens: Head of a family among the servants of Solomon who returned from exile
H2411.detail: Hatthil is a man who lived during the time of the exile and the return to Judea. He is mentioned as the head of a family of the descendants of the servants of King Solomon. In Ezra 2:57 and Nehemiah 7:59, he appears in the lists of those who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel after the destruction of the temple. His family was part of the lower classes attached to the service of the royal house before the exile.
H2411.origine: The name Hatthil (חַטִּיל) literally means "doubtful" or "uncertain." The exact etymology of the name remains debated among biblical scholars, but it appears exclusively in the lists of returnees from the Babylonian exile. The name is of Hebrew origin and characteristic of the post-exilic period.
H2411.emploi: Hatthil is mentioned exactly twice in the Hebrew Bible, both times in the lists of those who returned from captivity. In Ezra 2:57, he appears among the families of temple servants who accompanied Zerubbabel during the return from Babylon around 538 BC. The same passage is almost identically repeated in Nehemiah 7:59, where the lists are reiterated. In both cases, Hatthil is presented as the head of an entire family, indicating that he was a figure of some importance in the community of servants who returned from exile.

sens: Head of a family of temple servants who returned from exile with Zerubbabel
H2412.detail: Hathipha is the name of a man who lived at the time of the return from exile, during the time of Zerubbabel. He was the head of a family of temple servants ("temple slaves" in the source, meaning auxiliaries attached to the service of the Temple of Jerusalem). His name appears in the official lists of families who returned from Babylonian captivity to rebuild the Temple and restore the Jewish community in Jerusalem.
H2412.origine: The name Hathipha literally means "seized" or "taken away," which may evoke a circumstance of his birth or a significant event. It is a typical Hebrew name from the time of the return from exile.
H2412.emploi: Hathipha is mentioned only twice in the Bible, both in parallel genealogical lists: in Ezra 2:54 and Nehemiah 7:56. These two passages enumerate the families of temple servants who accompanied Zerubbabel during the return from Babylonian captivity. His name appears among those of the sons of Netsiach, indicating that he was the founder or representative of a lineage of temple servants officially recognized by the restored community.

sens: To master one's anger, to restrain one's wrath
To refrain from acting on one's impulse
H2413.detail:
1. The word literally means to hold something inside, to keep it locked up: it is to master a natural impulse that urges one to explode. Isaiah 48:9 speaks of God who restrains His anger for the honor of His name — instead of letting His indignation against a rebellious people run free, He holds back.

2. It is therefore an act of will: one resists the urge, one controls oneself, one refrains. This evokes the image of someone who tightens their lips or breathes deeply to avoid exploding with rage.
H2413.origine: The Hebrew verb חָטַם comes from a root that evokes the idea of closing, shutting, holding in. The word appears rarely in the Hebrew Bible. Its semantic family gathers the idea of containing, holding back what could escape — like holding water behind a dam or levee.
H2413.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 48:9, where it describes God's action of restraining (or refraining) His anger. The prophetic context shows God facing His unfaithful people: He would have legitimate reasons to punish, but He chooses to master Himself, to contain His righteous wrath, so as not to see His name dishonored. It is a rare word that emphasizes voluntary restraint in the face of provocation.
H2413.portee: For the believing reader, this verse reveals that God's patience is not indifference: it is an active force, a renewed choice to hold back His judgment out of love for His honor and mercy. It also invites the believer to meditate on their own ability to restrain themselves, to master their anger as God masters His.

sens: To seize someone or something by surprise and quickly
To carry away, to take by force, to steal
H2414.detail:
1. The word describes the action of seizing someone or something with a swift and unexpected gesture. It is the act of the hunter who catches his prey, or of the thief who takes his victim before they can react. In Psalms 10:9, the lion "surprises" the unfortunate one by springing from his hiding place, catching him when he least expects it.
2. Extended to the realm of abduction and violence, the word means to take someone away, to snatch them from their family to make them one's own. In Judges 21:21, the men of Benjamin "take away" the daughters of Shiloh, forcibly taking them to make them their wives — an act that the biblical context presents as serious and reprehensible.
H2414.origine: The Hebrew verb חָטַף (chaṭaph) expresses through imagery the sudden and unexpected gesture of one who seizes. The word belongs to the family of terms evoking sudden capture; it depicts less a calculated and slow action than a swift strike. Its basic meaning refers to the action of a predator or abductor who strikes without warning.
H2414.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible. In Judges 21:21, it refers to the abduction of the daughters of Shiloh by the Benjaminites, a dramatic event in the Old Testament where men without wives forcibly take young girls to marry them — a chaotic situation born out of civil war. In Psalms 10:9, the same verb depicts the lion springing from his lair to catch his prey, an image of the brutality of the wicked who lurk for the weak. The word always emphasizes the sudden and violent nature of the action.
H2414.portee: This word confronts us with the reality of abduction and violence in the Old Testament, and how the Bible does not hide these serious acts. It invites reflection on the protection of the weak and the sin of violence against those who cannot defend themselves. Meditating on these usages strengthens our awareness of the weight of sin and our gratitude for divine justice.

sens: Thin branch of a tree or plant
Stick or rod used as an instrument
Figure of descent or royalty
H2415.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a thin and flexible branch, like one that grows on a tree trunk — it is the natural and concrete image of the term. In Isaiah 11:1, the prophet speaks of a "branch" that will come forth from the stump of Jesse, evoking a young shoot that springs from a cut stump.
2. By extension, it can also refer to a stick or rod — an object used for correction or striking. In Proverbs 14:3, "a rod for his pride" means that the mouth of the fool feeds on words that nourish his own pride, or that bring blows upon him.
3. Figuratively, the branch represents royal or messianic descent — a new generation that grows from an ancient root. This is why Isaiah uses it to announce the Messiah who will be born from the line of David.
H2415.origine: The Hebrew word חֹטֵר (choter) comes from a root that evokes the idea of something thin, tender, and flexible — like a young branch that grows. It belongs to the family of words describing parts of a plant or elongated and thin objects. The term also has Semitic cousins that retain this sense of branch or stem.
H2415.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Proverbs 14:3, it is used to describe a rod — the object that expresses the verbal pride of the fool. In Isaiah 11:1, it takes on a prophetic and messianic dimension: the branch that comes from the stump of Jesse is one of the most famous images of the awaited Messiah, symbolizing the continuity of the royal line of David despite its apparent destruction. Between these two uses, the word shifts from the concrete sense (a rod, a branch) to the spiritual and politico-religious sense (the messianic dynasty).
H2415.portee: This word helps the reader understand how the Bible uses the image of nature to speak of spiritual and historical realities. The branch of Isaiah 11:1 teaches that, even when hope seems dead or cut off, God brings forth new life — a hope from the ruins. It is a promise of restoration and salvation that has profoundly marked both Jewish and Christian faith. For the Christian, it is the announcement of the Messiah from whom all new life proceeds.

sens: Having life, breathing and moving
In good condition, fresh and active (for a plant, water, a person)
Truly present, authentic, engaging (God, a promise)
Remaining alive after an event, survivor
H2416A.detail:
1. The simplest meaning: a creature or person endowed with life that functions, breathes, and acts. In Genesis 1:20, God creates the "living creatures" of the waters and the sky.
2. What is fresh, vigorous, and fully active. In Leviticus 13:16, we speak of "living flesh" — skin that is not dead or healed. A spring is "living" (running and pure water) when it gushes, not stagnant. Greenery is alive in the spring.
3. An affirmation of real and powerful presence, especially when one swears by something. Elijah says, "The Lord lives" (1 Kings 17:1): this is not an abstraction, it is God here and now, acting. It is a solid promise.
4. One who remains alive after death or danger. When someone is taken "alive" (1 Samuel 15:8), they are captured intact, not killed. Being "removed from the land of the living" (Psalms 52:7) means dying, ceasing to be counted among those who act.
H2416A.origine: The Hebrew word chay comes from a root that expresses the idea of vitality, driving force. In Hebrew, words of the same root concern the life that animates and vigor. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), this word is often translated as "zôon" or "zô" in Greek, which denote life as a dynamic and present principle.
H2416A.emploi: The word "living" appears more than 200 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the Torah and historical narratives. It primarily describes creatures and living beings (Genesis 1:20-30, Leviticus 11:46). It also qualifies what is fresh and active: a living water source, a "living" wound that oozes. In addition to these concrete uses, it becomes an affirmation: swearing "by the life of someone" or saying "God is living" is a way to solemnly engage one's word (1 Kings 17:1, Jeremiah 23:8). Finally, it distinguishes the survivors from the dead, those still present on earth. Its meaning varies little: it is always vitality, activity, real presence.
H2416A.portee: This word reminds us that life is never an abstraction for the Bible: it is the concrete reality of what breathes, acts, and renews. When the Bible says, "The Lord is living," it affirms that God is not a distant idea, but a dynamic presence that acts here and now. For the Christian, this means that faith is not a vague feeling, but a relationship with someone who is living, active, and reliable. It also invites us to recognize the sacred value of life in all its forms.

sens: Existence, the fact of living
The duration of a person's existence from birth to death
Active existence, the way of living
In a familial sense: kinship, lineage, clan
H2416B.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to existence itself, the fact of being alive as opposed to death. It is the concrete reality of living, breathing, acting in this world.
2. It can also be understood as the total duration of a human existence, from the first day to the last. This encompasses all the years, events, and experiences of a person.
3. The word also signifies the way of living, existence as it is conducted daily: how one acts, what one does, what one becomes. In 1 Samuel 18:18, when David asks Saul, "What is my life, what is my father's family," he refers to his own state, his condition as a person, his position in society relative to that of the king.
4. In relational contexts like this, the word can also evoke the clan, kinship, family heritage — what connects generations and gives each person their place in the people.
H2416B.origine: The Hebrew word חַי (chay) comes from a root that expresses the fact of being in motion, in activity, alive. The same word can refer to both a living creature and a person alive. It is a very ancient word, fundamental in biblical thought: life is the primary good, what distinguishes God's creatures from all that does not exist or is inert. Life appears in Genesis as God's central gift.
H2416B.emploi: The word "life" appears massively throughout the Hebrew Bible to evoke existence. In this unique use in 1 Samuel 18:18, David uses it to express his humble condition before the king: he wonders how a man of his condition, from an ordinary family, could become the son-in-law of a king. The word "life" there encompasses both personal existence and family clan, the social context. It is a formula of humility: David highlights the insignificance of his importance compared to that of the king.
H2416B.portee: This exchange shows that David, despite God's royal choice upon him, remains aware of his humble status and dependence. He does not allow himself to be swayed by the growing favor but recognizes the social distances. For the reader, this reveals a humble heart, a distancing from honors — a lesson in wisdom and restraint, a prerequisite for true leadership.

sens: Living creature endowed with flesh and blood, distinct from humans, plants, and celestial beings
Wild or dangerous creature, formidable
Earthly creature understood as God's creation and subject to His order
Small creature, insignificant being
Principle of life, vital appetite or animal instinct
H2416C.detail: 1. The word primarily designates any warm-blooded living being: quadruped, reptile, bird. Genesis 1:24 uses it to describe the creatures that God commands the earth to produce according to their kind — the context of Creation reveals that the animal is a distinct category, subject to human authority (Genesis 2:19-20). 2. It also applies to fierce or harmful beasts: in Genesis 37:33, Jacob believes his son was devoured by a "wild beast"; the psalms speak of beasts that threaten the faithful (Psalms 79:2). 3. Sometimes the word includes creatures within God's design: in Ezekiel 1:13-22, the "animals" are the celestial beings of the divine chariot, reminding us that all living creation glorifies the Lord (Psalms 104:11, 148:10). 4. The word can denote an insignificant creature, almost contemptible: Jeremiah 12:9 refers to birds as "beasts" in a context of profanation. 5. Rarely, "animal" evokes carnal appetite or vital vigor (Isaiah 57:10 speaks of fatigue and "appetite").
H2416C.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to live" (חיה), from which the verb "to be alive" derives. An animal is literally what "lives" and breathes. The word has a concrete and lively connotation: it designates what moves, breathes, and has a soul (nephesh). In Aramaic, the parallel form is חֵיוָא ("beast"), which appears in the prophetic visions of Daniel.
H2416C.emploi: The word "animal" appears 98 times in the Bible, mainly in Genesis, Leviticus, Ezekiel, and Psalms. In Genesis 1-2, it describes the order of Creation and humanity's dominion. In the Levitical code, it distinguishes clean animals from unclean ones (Leviticus 11:2, 11:27). In Isaiah and Jeremiah, it becomes a symbol of threat or divine judgment: wild beasts will devastate the rebellious land (Leviticus 26:22, Isaiah 35:9). In Job and the Psalms, the animal is integrated into divine providence: God nourishes and cares for them (Psalms 50:10, 104:11, 104:25). In Ezekiel, the "animals" of the throne vision are the celestial beings of God's glorious chariot.
H2416C.portee: This word invites the believer to recognize that all created life comes from God and belongs to Him. In Genesis, the animal reminds us that humans are not alone in creation but are responsible for it. The prophetic warnings show that when the people rebel against God, even the creatures turn against them. Finally, the Psalms teach us to praise God alongside the animals — a lesson in humility: we are but a part of His glorious creation.

sens: Group of people gathered or organized
Whole of the people, community
Existence, life
H2416D.detail:
1. A troop designates a group of people who come together for a common action: in 2 Samuel 23:13, it is a band of warriors who come down to David during the harvest, or an army of Philistines camped in the valley. The word evokes the idea of unity and collective strength.
2. More broadly, this term can refer to the people as a whole, the entire community: in Psalms 68:11, the "people" establishes its dwelling in the land that God has prepared, showing how a troop becomes a unified and organized body.
3. In a rarer sense, closer to the original Hebrew word, the term can also mean the life or existence of a group: in Psalms 74:19, God is called not to forget "the life of your afflicted ones," where the common life of the poor people is placed under divine protection.
H2416D.origine: The Hebrew word חַיָּה (chay.yah) is related to the root חָיָה (chayah) which means "to live" or "to make live." Literally, it thus designates a "living community" or a "group of living beings." This etymology reveals that for the Hebrews, a troop or a people is primarily a collection of beings who share life together. The word is rooted in the concrete image of collective life, of common existence.
H2416D.emploi: This Hebrew word appears four times in the Old Testament, always to describe a group of people. In 2 Samuel 23:11 and 23:13, it qualifies a military troop — first a band of fighters who bring water to David, then the Philistine army camped in the valley. In Psalms 68:11, it designates the chosen people as a whole, established in the land of God. In Psalms 74:19, it takes on a different nuance: the "life" of the afflicted, where the word shifts towards the meaning of existence and destiny of a class of people. The usage thus varies between a specific military unit and the entire community, always with the idea of shared life.
H2416D.portee: This word reminds the believer that God sees and protects not only individuals but also groups, communities, and peoples. When the Bible speaks of troops or peoples, it affirms that collective existence is precious in God's eyes — whether it concerns warriors serving a king or the forgotten afflicted of the world. This invites Christians to regard communal life as sacred and to recognize that God never abandons a people that turns to Him.

sens: Human existence, the fact of living
The duration of a person's life, their days and years
What allows one to live, sustenance and maintenance
Life as a precious good, to be cherished and prolonged
In a figurative sense, spiritual existence and the relationship with God
H2416E.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the fundamental fact that we are alive, in contrast to death. It is the breath that animates the body: when God "breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, man became a living being" (Genesis 2:7). Without this divine breath, there is only inert dust.

2. It also refers to the concrete duration of our days: "all the days of your life," is the response given to the psalmist who asks how much time he has left (Deuteronomy 4:9). Life is a succession of years to be counted — a man lives so many years, then dies.

3. The word also evokes what nourishes and sustains us: the daily bread, the conditions that maintain our existence. This is why we speak of "maintenance" or sustenance in certain passages.

4. The Bible treats life as a precious gift that can be multiplied or lost, accumulated or squandered. One "keeps oneself during one's life" (Proverbs 9:11), one "cherishes life" or "refuses it".

5. Often, "life" refers to the relationship with God Himself: "in His presence is fullness of joy; at His right hand are pleasures forevermore" (Psalms 16:11). It is a spiritual life, not reducible to mere heartbeats.
H2416E.origine: The Hebrew word חַיִּים (chay.yim) comes from a root that means "to live" or "to be alive." It is a plural: literally "the lives," an emphatic formulation that underscores the intensity and importance of the concept. The word concretely designates what animates a being — the breath, the energy, the warmth. The root is found in verbs like "to be alive" and nouns like "living creature." In the Greek Old Testament, this word often translates the Greek ζωή (zôé), which also carries the idea of a vital force at work.
H2416E.emploi: The word "life" appears about 137 times in the received Hebrew text. It is found everywhere: in Genesis where it describes the animation of man and all animals, in the Law (Deuteronomy) where it exhorts the people to "choose life" (30:19), in the Psalms where the believer cries out, "Lord, You are my life" (27:1), and in the wisdom books (Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Job) that reflect on the duration and quality of our days. The word encompasses several nuances: sometimes it refers to raw animal life ("all living flesh"), sometimes human life with its consciousness and responsibility ("the days of your life"), and sometimes the very existence of the people as a community (Rehoboam and Jeroboam "as long as Rehoboam lived"). The context always affects the depth of meaning.
H2416E.portee: For the believer, understanding that life comes from God and remains a constant gift transforms everything. It is not a possession to be taken for granted. It calls for gratitude, respectful fear, and moral vigilance: "take heed to yourself and watch over your soul" (Deuteronomy 4:9). The Psalmist did not settle for merely "living"; he sought "life" in the fullest sense — communion with God. Choosing "life" in Deuteronomy means choosing to obey the Word of God, which alone nourishes the soul beyond mere survival.

sens: Having life, breathing and moving
Existing truly, subsisting
Acting with power and active presence
Life, existence
H2417.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes one who possesses physical life, who is alive and not dead. In Daniel 2:30, the king seeks among all the "living" for someone who could explain his dream: it is a call to all human beings who breathe and live.
2. It also qualifies what exists truly and remains, in contrast to what is vain or perishable. When Nebuchadnezzar praises "Him who lives forever" (Daniel 4:34), he acknowledges that only God possesses eternal and indestructible existence.
3. The word can express the idea of an active and powerful presence: "the living God" (Daniel 6:20, 6:26) means not only that God exists, but that He acts, intervenes, and shows effectiveness in the affairs of men, unlike the mute or absent gods of idols.
4. "Life" also denotes existence itself, as in Ezra 6:10 where prayer is made for the king's "life," meaning for his prosperity and longevity.
H2417.origine: The Hebrew word חַי (chay) comes from a root that means "to live" or "to breathe." The Aramaic chay is a related form, used in the Aramaic portions of the book of Daniel and Ezra. This root expresses the fundamental idea of movement, breathing, and active presence: a living being is one who moves and acts, in contrast to the dead who are immobile. The same root appears in many Hebrew and Aramaic words related to life.
H2417.emploi: This Aramaic word appears 7 times in the Old Testament, exclusively in the Aramaic portions of Daniel and Ezra (chapters 2-7 of Daniel and certain passages in Ezra). There are three major uses: first, it qualifies living beings or humans ("all the living" in Daniel 2:30 and 4:17); next, it characterizes God as "living" or "eternal" (Daniel 4:34, 6:20, 6:26), which emphasizes His reality, power, and permanent presence in the face of worldly powers; finally, it can mean life itself as a precious good (Ezra 6:10). The context slightly alters according to the passages: sometimes it is an affirmation of what truly exists, sometimes a recognition of divine power.
H2417.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reveals something essential: the God of the Bible is not an abstract idea, a distant or static deity, but a living God who acts and responds. Nebuchadnezzar, the great king of Babylon, learns this to his cost and proclaims: He who "lives forever" reigns over the kingdoms of men (Daniel 4:34). It is a call to recognize that our faith rests on an encounter with a real, present, and powerful God, not on vain superstitions.

sens: To exist, to breathe, to remain alive
To grant or maintain life to someone
To last long, to persist in existence
To enjoy life, to inhabit a certain state
H2418.detail:
1. The primary meaning is simply to exist and remain alive, as expressed in the Aramaic phrase "O king, live forever" (Daniel 2:4): a wish that the king continues to breathe and reign without end.
2. The verb also carries the meaning of allowing to live or granting life: in chapter 5 of Daniel, the king "allowed life to those he wished," meaning he spared some from death and kept them alive by his sovereign authority.
3. The expression "to live forever" suggests an infinite duration, an existence that persists uninterrupted through time.
H2418.origine: The word comes from the Aramaic root חיה (haya), which expresses vital breath and animated existence. It is the fundamental verb of life, very close to the Hebrew word חַיִּים (hayim, "life"). In Aramaic, it can take different forms that add nuances: the simple form means "to live," while other forms can express the idea of making live or maintaining alive.
H2418.emploi: This verb appears six times in Aramaic in the book of Daniel, almost exclusively in chapters 2, 3, 5, and 6. Four times, it appears in the solemn address of courtiers, Chaldean sages, or Daniel himself to the king: "O king, live forever!" It is a formula of respect and goodwill towards the sovereign, as a prayer that he may enjoy his power for a long time. Only once (Daniel 5:19), the verb takes on the active meaning of "to allow to live," describing the king's power over his subjects: he kills or spares according to his will. Everywhere, the context is political and royal.
H2418.portee: This word reminds us that life is a precious gift, not a guaranteed possession. Among pagan kings, the right to dispose of life is an absolute power; for the believer, it is the Lord alone who holds life and death in His hands. The phrase "live forever" also expresses the human aspiration to transcend death, an aspiration that only God can fulfill.

sens: Man from Bethel who rebuilt Jericho during the reign of Ahab
H2419.detail: Hiel is a man from Bethel who, during the time of the divided monarchy (under Ahab, king of Israel), undertook to rebuild the city of Jericho. This action had a terrible consequence: according to the curse pronounced long ago by Joshua at the first destruction of Jericho, the rebuilding of the city cost the lives of his two sons, Abiram and Segub, the first during the laying of the foundations and the second during the installation of the gates. This event illustrates how God's word is fulfilled across generations, even long after it was spoken.
H2419.origine: The name Hiel means "God sees" or "God is alive," composed of Hebrew elements denoting God and life. He is an obscure man from the time of the divided monarchy in Israel, mentioned only once in Scripture, but in a very significant way since his action illustrates the fulfillment of the word spoken by Joshua.
H2419.emploi: Hiel appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 16:34. The account presents him as a builder of Jericho during the reign of Ahab (approximately 870-851 B.C.). The mention of this event in the royal history of Israel emphasizes how the curse proclaimed by Joshua centuries earlier (see Joshua 6:26, where Joshua declares cursed anyone who rebuilds Jericho) was fulfilled through the personal drama of this man. It is a striking example of the faithfulness and certainty of God's word.
H2419.portee: The story of Hiel teaches that God's word does not fail: a curse pronounced generations earlier was fulfilled when Hiel undertook to rebuild Jericho. It invites the reader to take God's warnings seriously and to recognize that His word will infallibly come to pass, even if long after it was spoken. It is a call to trust in the certainty of the promises and warnings of the Lord.

sens: Obscure and mysterious word, difficult to understand
Question posed to be solved, brain teaser
Saying or proverb formulated in an enigmatic way
Veiled allegory or parable
H2420.detail: 1. A hidden word or speech that requires interpretation: God tells Moses that He does not speak to him "without riddles" (Numbers 12:8), meaning that He speaks clearly with Moses, not through riddles as with other prophets who receive veiled visions. 2. A difficult question posed to test intelligence: Samson poses a riddle to his wedding companions in exchange for thirty garments (Judges 14:12-13); the queen of Sheba comes to test Solomon with riddles (2 Chronicles 9:1). 3. A maxim or saying presented in an enigmatic form: Psalm 49:5 announces that he will speak in riddles, mixing wisdom and proverbs. 4. A cryptic allegory or parable that contains a hidden meaning: Ezekiel 17:2 announces that he will propose a riddle to the house of Israel, meaning a symbolic story to decipher.
H2420.origine: The Hebrew word חִידָה (chidah) comes from the root חוד (chuud) which evokes the idea of diverting, tying, or binding in secret. A riddle "ties" the meaning, enveloping it to hide it. In Aramaic, אֲחִידָה (achidah) has the same meaning. The word refers to the image of something that is not stated plainly, but intertwined, mixed in a way that requires ingenuity to unravel.
H2420.emploi: The word appears 17 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in wisdom and prophetic narratives. In Judges, the riddle is a game: Samson proposes one to his companions (Judges 14:13-19), and it is appealing enough that they seek to solve it. In wisdom literature, it becomes a pedagogical tool: Solomon is famous for solving them (1 Kings 10:1; 2 Chronicles 9:1), and the wise person who speaks in riddles conveys a teaching that requires reflection (Proverbs 1:6). Among the prophets (Ezekiel, Habakkuk, Daniel), the riddle takes the form of a vision or an allegory to interpret: it is God's veiled word that demands discernment.
H2420.portee: The riddle reminds us that divine wisdom is not always revealed at first glance. It invites the reader to think deeply, to seek further, rather than to accept the first meaning that comes to mind. It also shows that God can speak in hidden ways—not out of malice, but to invite the listener to engage actively with His word, to be shaped by the search for deeper meaning.

sens: To have life, to be alive, to continue to exist
To remain alive, to survive in a dangerous or precarious situation
To subsist, to feed oneself, to live off something
To prosper, to live in ease and blessing
To come back to life, to heal, to recover
To give life to someone, to make them live or survive
H2421.detail:
1. To have life, to be alive, to continue to exist: this is the most fundamental meaning, that of possessing life and remaining alive. In Genesis 3:22, Adam and Eve are not to "live forever" — they risk eating from the tree of life and becoming immortal. The genealogies in Genesis 5 repeatedly say, "X lived so many years": "to live" simply means to go through one's days of existence.
2. To remain alive, to survive in a dangerous or precarious situation: when life is threatened, "to live" becomes an act of defense. Lot pleads, "Let my soul live!" (Genesis 19:20), fleeing from the disaster of Sodom. Cain tells Abram, "Say that you are my brother, so that my soul may live" (Genesis 12:13) — a request for protection to avoid being killed.
3. To subsist, to feed oneself, to live off something: "to live" also includes the ability to sustain oneself. In Genesis 47:19, the Egyptians offer their lands to Pharaoh "so that we may live" — they agree to become servants in exchange for food and survival.
4. To prosper, to live in ease and blessing: beyond mere existence, "to live" can mean to enjoy a good life. In Deuteronomy 16:20, "you will live and possess the land" — to live is to enjoy stability and God's promises.
5. To come back to life, to heal, to recover: when someone suffers or weakens, to restore or heal them is called "to make live." In 2 Kings 8:9, Hazael asks, "Will I recover from this illness?" — literally "Will I live?" — in Hebrew it is a single notion: to regain health is to come back to life.
6. To give or preserve life: this meaning appears when an active verb "makes someone live." Pharaoh orders the midwives to kill the male newborns, but they "make the children live" (Exodus 1:17) — they let them live and save them.
H2421.origine: The verb חָיָה (chayah) comes from a root that evokes the idea of warmth, vitality, and breath — what makes a creature alive. The Hebrew word חַיִּים (chayyim, "life") derives from the same root and appears hundreds of times in the Bible, notably in Genesis 2 with "the tree of life." The root is very ancient and common to other Semitic languages. In English, our translations "to live" and "life" faithfully reflect the closeness of the Greek ζάω (zaô) and ζωή (zôê), which translate this verb in the Greek version of the Old Testament.
H2421.emploi: This verb is one of the most frequent in the Hebrew Bible — 257 occurrences in total. It appears as early as Genesis 3 and extends everywhere, especially in the narratives of Genesis and Exodus where it describes the lifespan of the patriarchs. Used alone, "to live" simply describes the fact of being alive or continuing to exist: the genealogies of Genesis 5 repeat it mechanically ("Abraham lived 175 years"). With a richer value, it means to survive a danger (Lot fleeing Sodom) or to subsist (the Egyptians serving Pharaoh to eat). With an object, it can express "to live off" something. Formed in the passive or with a subject that undergoes the action, it denotes healing or restoration (coming from illness to health). Used in the imperative or in the subjunctive, it expresses the ardent desire to live or to see someone live ("let my soul live!"). Deuteronomy often links it to righteousness and blessing: "If you observe my law, you will live."
H2421.portee: This word evokes all that enriches the relationship of man to the Eternal: the dependence of life on God, who alone is the source and guarantor of life, and the promise that following His commandments is the way to true, lasting, and blessed life. It also reminds us that life is a precious gift that God preserves, but also takes back; that is why Scripture constantly exhorts to "choose life." For a Christian, this verb takes on a new dimension in Jesus: "I am the resurrection and the life" — Jesus alone gives eternal life to those who believe in Him.

sens: Having physical strength, vigor
Being in good health, robust
Full of life and energy
H2422.detail:
1. The word describes a person or an animal that possesses remarkable physical strength, capable of exerting intense effort. In Exodus 1:19, the Egyptian midwives describe the Hebrew women as "vigorous," meaning robust and strong, which explains why they give birth easily without medical assistance.
2. It is also the state of one who enjoys good health, without weakness or illness. This meaning encompasses the idea that life itself flows abundantly in the veins — one is "alive" in the strong sense of the term.
3. The word can apply to what is animated, active, vibrant with life — opposed to fatigue, exhaustion, or approaching death.
H2422.origine: The Hebrew word comes from the root חיה (chayah), which means "to live" or "to be alive." It is a derived adjective that retains this fundamental idea: one who is vigorous is fully alive, life expresses itself fully in them. The root itself evokes the idea of vitality, breath, and life force. Words from the same family describe life (חַיִּים, chayim) or one who lives (חָי, chay).
H2422.emploi: This word appears only once in the Old Testament, in Exodus 1:19. The Egyptian midwives use it to respond to Pharaoh's suspicions: if the Hebrew male children were being born so numerous without their help, it is because the Hebrew mothers were "vigorous," meaning in excellent physical health and endowed with great strength. This context shows that the word particularly applies to a concrete and observable physical capacity — the strength and robustness of the body.
H2422.portee: This word reminds us that health and vigor are blessings from the Lord. Among the Hebrew women, this strength was a sign of divine blessing that preserved them and prepared them to fulfill their role in the history of salvation. It is also an invitation to see in life, health, and strength an expression of God's goodness toward His people.

sens: Living creature with a body that moves
Animal with a wild temperament or instincts
Creature subjected to man, lacking reason
Mythical or prophetic beast
Man degraded to an animal state
H2423.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to any living creature that walks, from the smallest to the largest. In Daniel 2:38, God places under the control of the king "the beasts of the fields and the birds of the heavens" — in other words, all terrestrial and aerial animals.

2. A beast is often wild or fierce, capable of devouring or dominating. The four beasts of Daniel 7 — leopard, lion, bear — embody brutal and destructive powers.

3. The beast also represents the domestic animal or the being without reason, incapable of speaking or thinking like a man. In Daniel 4:15 and 4:23, the king is ordered to "share the grass of the earth with the beasts," a metaphor for total humiliation.

4. In prophetic visions, particularly in Daniel 7, the beasts become symbols of kingdoms or political powers in conflict — a common usage in biblical apocalyptic literature.

5. Finally, the word can describe a man reduced to living like an animal, stripped of his human dignity. Nebuchadnezzar, in Daniel 5:21, was "driven from among the children of men" and his "heart was made like that of the beasts": he ate like oxen and lived with wild donkeys.
H2423.origine: The Aramaic word חֵיוָא (cheva) comes from the same root as the Hebrew חַיָּה (chayah), which literally means "living" or "living creature." This root expresses the idea of movement and animal life. In biblical Hebrew, חַיָּה also refers to terrestrial animals as opposed to birds. The word is common in both languages of the ancient Near East to denote any living being lacking reason.
H2423.emploi: This Aramaic word appears exclusively in the book of Daniel (19 occurrences), which was partially written in Aramaic, the administrative language of the Babylonian and Persian empires. It is used literally to describe the animals of the fields and the earth (Daniel 2:38, 4:15, 4:23), all creatures subjected to man. But its most striking usage is prophetic and symbolic: in the visions of Daniel 7, four successive beasts arise from the sea, representing empires or kingdoms that succeed and oppose each other (the lion, the bear, the leopard, and a fourth terrifying beast). Finally, the word takes on a moral and theological value when it qualifies the humiliated Nebuchadnezzar: his heart "was made like that of the beasts" (Daniel 5:21), expressing the degradation of the sovereign reduced to an animal state for having forgotten God.
H2423.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on the hierarchy of creation: the beast is the animal, created to serve man or to symbolize hostile powers. Daniel's visions teach that earthly kingdoms, no matter how powerful they may be, are beasts in the eyes of God — creatures subjected to His judgment and eternal authority. The image of the heart becoming "like that of the beasts" reminds us that pride and rebellion against God degrade man, while humility and acknowledgment of His sovereignty elevate him.

sens: state of life, existence
condition of one who lives
way of living, lifestyle
H2424.detail:
1. The word denotes the fundamental state of one who exists and breathes, in contrast to death. In 2 Samuel 20:3, David's concubines remain "living" — that is, still alive — but in a miserable situation, confined and without hope of marriage: it emphasizes that they exist physically, even though their lives are broken.
2. More broadly, it characterizes the condition of one who is alive, their state of existence. The word emphasizes less the simple fact of breathing than the status of a person alive — a living being in the eyes of others, someone who continues their existence in the world.
3. It can also evoke the concrete manner in which one lives, the circumstances of existence. Here, the concubines live in confinement and maintenance, far from any freedom — the word encompasses both that they are alive and how they live.
H2424.origine: The word comes from the root חיה (chaya), which means "to live" or "to be alive." This root is one of the most fundamental in biblical Hebrew, expressing vital existence. The form חַיּוּת is an abstract noun derived from the same root: it names the state or quality of one who lives — similar to how the French "chaleur" comes from the verb "chauffer." It is also found in common words like חַי (chai), "living," which appears throughout Scripture.
H2424.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 2 Samuel 20:3. It is a rare term, used to express in both a simple and striking way that these women, although confined and deprived of marital life, remain alive — an existence that endures despite misfortune. This uniqueness of usage suggests that the author sought a discreet yet rich word to name the raw state of life in which these concubines languished.
H2424.portee: This word reminds us that life itself — the simple fact of living — is a gift from God, but also that living is not enough: one can exist physically while losing the fruits and freedom that give meaning to existence. For the reader, it is an invitation not to confuse mere survival with a full life, according to God's will.

sens: To have life, to exist, to breathe
To remain alive, to continue to exist
To live prosperously, to enjoy life
To return to life, to be restored from illness or weakness
To give life, to allow someone to live
To revive, restore, reinvigorate
H2425.detail:
1. To have life, to exist: this is the most fundamental meaning, designating the simple fact of being alive, breathing, possessing life. In 1 Samuel 20:31, Saul says, "as long as the son of Jesse is alive on the earth," he was speaking of David who still exists, who has not been killed.
2. To remain alive, to continue to exist: this is to persevere in life, to maintain one's existence against the threats of death. This is what Saul fears upon seeing David still alive.
3. To live prosperously: beyond mere existence, this means to enjoy life, to live happily and securely, with a full and satisfying life.
4. To return to life, to be restored: to recover from illness, discouragement, or great weakness, to regain vigor and health.
5. To give life, to allow someone to live: this is the action of preserving life, letting live, maintaining someone who might otherwise die.
6. To revive, restore: this is to rekindle what has gone out, to give strength and vigor back to one who was weakened or downcast.
H2425.origine: The Hebrew word חָיַי (chayay) comes from a root that fundamentally expresses the idea of life, vitality, and movement. This verb is at the very heart of biblical thought on existence. The family of the word includes חַיִּים (chaïm, "life"), חַי (chaï, "living"), and denotes what is active, dynamic, and full of energy. Life, in the Bible, is never passive: it is a reality that breathes, acts, and persists.
H2425.emploi: The verb "to live" (chayay) carries rich nuances in the Bible depending on the context. It first describes the simple fact of existing and remaining alive in the face of threats (as in 1 Samuel 20:31, where Saul fears that David continues to live and threatens his power). It can also mean to live long, to live in peace and security, or to enjoy a happy life. Finally, it carries a sense of restoration and renewal: to return to life after illness, to be revived after discouragement, or to be resurrected after death. This last sense prepares the reader to understand God's power over life and death.
H2425.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that life comes from God and remains under His control. To live is not just to breathe: it is to exist in relationship with God, enjoying His blessing and protection. The verb "to live" also evokes the possibility of restoration, inner renewal, and spiritual resurrection. It is a word of hope: even when one is downcast, weakened, or desperate, God can revive us and restore us to life.

sens: Fortified structure built around a city or fortress for defense
City wall, enclosing wall
Army, military troop (figurative or extended sense)
H2426.detail:
