This word also invites vigilance: not to mix the sacred and the profane is to honor God by maintaining the appropriate separation.

sens: to suffer physically from an illness
to be afflicted with a bodily ailment
to experience a lasting infirmity or pain
H2456.detail:
1. The word describes the state of a person who suffers from a physical illness. It is the concrete experience of pain and bodily discomfort. In 2 Chronicles 16:12, King Asa "had diseased feet": his feet were afflicted with an ailment that caused him great suffering.
2. Beyond mere temporary discomfort, the word evokes a lasting condition, an infirmity that afflicts the person. The example of King Asa shows that it was a suffering serious enough to mark his life and reign, even while he was afflicted.
H2456.origine: The Hebrew root חלא (cha-la) expresses the idea of suffering and illness. It is related to the ancient Semitic world where illness was perceived as an affliction to the integrity of the body. The word can also express debility, the physical weakening that accompanies serious illness. This root appears in the biblical context as an inevitable human reality, without necessarily carrying a moral judgment.
H2456.emploi: This verb appears rarely in the Hebrew Bible. The only attested use in the Segond (2 Chronicles 16:12) describes the illness of King Asa, struck by an infirmity in his feet. The context underscores the irony: although gravely ill, the king preferred to consult physicians rather than seek the Lord. This historical narrative uses the word to show how a physical trial reveals a person's heart.
H2456.portee: The illness of King Asa teaches that bodily affliction is an opportunity to turn to God. When we suffer, we are invited to seek the Lord first rather than relying solely on our human or medical resources. This example reminds us that illness can be a call to examine our hearts and return to dependence on God.

sens: The oxide that forms on the surface of a metal and dirties it
The deposit of dirt or residue accumulated on something
Figuratively: the moral stain or sin that accumulates
H2457.detail:
1. The word literally denotes rust, that brownish oxide that forms and embeds itself on metal. In Ezekiel 24:6, the city is described as a "cauldron full of rust," an image of what accumulates and defiles.
2. More broadly, it refers to any dirty deposit or residue that increases on the surface: rust does not "detach" easily (Ezekiel 24:6), it must be consumed by fire (Ezekiel 24:11), so deeply does it adhere and root itself.
3. Figuratively, the prophet uses this image to speak of the moral stain and sin accumulated in the city: just as rust can only be removed by the intense heat of fire, Israel's guilt can only be removed by God's judgment.
H2457.origine: The Hebrew word chel'ah comes from a root that expresses the idea of accumulation and crust. Its basic image is that of a deposit that aggregates and hardens on the surface of an object, forming a tenacious layer. It is a concrete term from the material world, used by Ezekiel to speak of what thickens and adheres.
H2457.emploi: The word appears only three times, all in chapter 24 of Ezekiel, where the prophet pronounces an oracle against Jerusalem. The cauldron represents the city; the rust is first its criminal content ("cauldron full of rust"), then becomes the symbol of the moral stain that has accumulated there. In verses 6, 11, and 12, Ezekiel emphasizes the tenacious and inescapable nature of this stain: it can only be consumed by intense fire, an image of inevitable divine judgment. The word embodies the idea that sin takes root and demands radical punishment.
H2457.portee: This biblical image shows that sin does not disappear through superficial efforts or partial attempts at improvement. Like rust that embeds deeply, guilt accumulates and solidifies. It invites the reader to recognize that only intense divine judgment or purification can truly remove the stain from the heart. It is a call to serious repentance rather than cosmetic reforms.

sens: woman of the tribe of Judah during the time of the divided monarchy
one of the two wives of Ashur
mother of Zereth, Izhar, Ethnan, and Koz
H2458.detail: Helea is a woman of Judah mentioned in the genealogies of the book of Chronicles. She is one of the two wives of Ashur, who is presented as the father of Tekoa (1 Chronicles 4:5). She had four sons: Zereth, Izhar, Ethnan, and Koz, listed in 1 Chronicles 4:7. Her name appears in the genealogical lists of Judah, which trace the descendants of the tribes of Israel during the time when the kingdom was divided between the north and the south.
H2458.origine: The name Helea means "rust" in Hebrew. It is an ancient Hebrew feminine name borne by this figure in the Judean genealogy. Although the literal meaning of the name is rarely used in biblical contexts, it reflects the poetic or descriptive names found in the families of ancient Israel.
H2458.emploi: Helea appears only twice in the Bible, both in 1 Chronicles 4, which lists the genealogies of the tribe of Judah. She is first mentioned in 1 Chronicles 4:5 as one of the two women of Ashur, alongside Naara. Then in 1 Chronicles 4:7, her four sons are listed. These two verses are the only passages that mention her in all of Scripture.

sens: The fatty substance of the bodies of animals and humans
What is removed from the entrails and chest of the sacrificed animals
The richest and most flavorful part of food
What is abundant, prosperous, fruitful
The image of what is rich and satisfying, in a spiritual sense
H2459.detail:
1. It primarily refers to physical fat, the adipose tissue of animals and humans: when Cain presents to the Lord "from their fat" taken from the firstborn of his flock (Genesis 4:4), he offers the most precious portion of the animal.
2. In the sacrificial worship, "fat" specifically refers to the fats taken from the entrails and around the kidneys, on the chest (Leviticus 3:16; 9:20): this is what the priest burns on the altar as "food of a sacrifice consumed by fire."
3. The word can also mean the best, the richest: Genesis 45:18 promises "the best of the land of Egypt," and Psalms 81:17 speaks of the "wheat" and the "honey from the rock," images of blessing.
4. "Fat" evokes abundance and prosperity: a "fat" land is fertile and generous.
5. Spiritually, having a heart "thickened" or "covered with fat" (Psalms 119:70) means being closed off, insensitive to the words of God — fat then becomes a symbol of hardening and selfishness.
H2459.origine: The Hebrew word חֵלֶב (chélev) refers to visible fat, particularly that which envelops the organs. It comes from a root related to the idea of covering, enveloping — which well reflects how fat covers the body. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, στέαρ (stéar) is often found. The Law formally stipulates the prohibition of consuming the fat of certain animals (Leviticus 7:23), as it is reserved for the Lord, burned on the altar as an offering.
H2459.emploi: The word "fat" appears 69 times in the Bible, mainly in Leviticus and the historical books. It is primarily a term of worship: almost half of the occurrences describe the ritual of sacrifices, where the fat of the victim is burned on the altar as a portion offered to God (notably Leviticus 3 and 4). The Law commands the Israelites not to eat the fat of the ox, the lamb, or the goat (Leviticus 7:23-25) — it belongs to the Lord alone. The word then takes on a broader meaning: it signifies the abundance and richness of the land (Genesis 45:18; Psalms 147:14 speaks of "wheat" and honey). Finally, it acquires a spiritual dimension: in the Psalms, the fat thickening the heart represents moral and spiritual insensitivity (Psalms 17:10; 119:70), hardening in the face of God's will.
H2459.portee: For the believer, the word "fat" reminds us that God demands the best and the most precious — never the refuse or mediocrity. In sacrificial worship, the fat burned on the altar illustrates how we offer to God what we have that is richest, as a sign of love and submission. Spiritually, the warning against a heart "covered with fat" invites us to remain vigilant, attentive to the voice of God, without falling asleep in comfort or selfishness. It is a call to the refinement of heart and conscience.

sens: Warrior in the service of King David, son of Baanah
H2460.detail: Heleb is one of the mighty warriors of King David, mentioned in the list of his "mighty men" (2 Samuel 23:29). He is the son of Baanah, from the city of Nethopha. He is a renowned fighter, one of those who served the king and earned his trust through their courage in battle.
H2460.origine: The name Heleb literally means "milk" in Hebrew, likely given to the child for a personal reason from his family that we do not know. Another warrior of the time bears a similar name, Heleth or Heldaï, indicating that the name had variations in the text tradition. The name belongs to the time of the united kingdom under David and Solomon.
H2460.emploi: Heleb is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Samuel 23:29, in the official list of David's "mighty men" or "valiant men" — thirty-seven warriors who marked his reign. This list honors those who fought for the king and supported him militarily. His appearance in this enumeration indicates that he was a figure of some military importance in the united kingdom.

sens: White liquid produced by the mammary glands of animals, particularly cows and goats, used for nourishment.
Dairy products such as cheese or curds.
Whiteness or white color, compared to that of milk.
Abundance and fertility of the promised land (poetic image).
Basic food, symbol of sustenance and provision.
H2461.detail:
1. Milk is the white liquid produced by domesticated animals. In Genesis 18:8, Abraham offers milk to his heavenly visitors, which was a valuable gift. It is a daily food, as evidenced by Proverbs 27:27: "The milk of the goats is sufficient for your food." Milk was also preserved as cheese, hence the occasional translation of the word as "cheese." 
2. Sour or curdled milk, and cheese, are preserved forms of milk. Although rare in our usage, this meaning appears in the translation since Exodus 34:26 speaks of "not boiling a kid in its mother's milk"—a prohibition concerning a dairy product. 
3. The whiteness of milk serves as a comparison: Lamentations 4:7 describes a person's limbs as "whiter than milk," evoking purity or bright whiteness. 
4. The expression "a land flowing with milk and honey" (Deuteronomy 11:9, Joshua 5:6) paints a picture of a land of abundance and fertility. Milk symbolizes prosperous herds and wealth in livestock. 
5. Milk represents simple yet vital food. In Isaiah 55:1, the prophet invites the hungry to buy "wine and milk"—essential provisions offered freely by God.
H2461.origine: The Hebrew word חָלָב (chalav) is an ancient root designating animal milk. It does not have a particularly rich variant in the same language, but it belongs to the vocabulary of shepherds and herders in the Semitic world. Milk was then a product of primary importance in Mediterranean and Middle Eastern diets, hence the significance of the word in biblical texts. Its metaphorical use (abundance, whiteness, fertility) shows how precious and familiar this product was to the people of Israel.
H2461.emploi: The word appears 44 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the legislative and prophetic books. It primarily designates animal milk: Abraham offers it to his guests (Genesis 18:8), it can be used to cook the calf (Exodus 34:26), and shepherds bring it to David (1 Samuel 17:18). Very often, it appears in the expression "a land flowing with milk and honey" to describe the Promised Land (Deuteronomy 11:9, Joshua 5:6, Numbers 13:27, Ezekiel 20:6)—an image of blessed abundance. The word is also used to refer to other forms: curdled or sour cheese. Rarely, it describes whiteness (Lamentations 4:7). Each usage emphasizes either concrete sustenance or divine promise.
H2461.portee: Milk reminds the believer that God provides for the concrete needs of His people. The image of the land "flowing with milk and honey" invites trust in His promise of abundance. For the Christian reader, milk can also evoke the simple yet nourishing spiritual food that Scripture offers to the children of God, particularly to the younger ones in faith.

sens: City in the territory of Asher, near Sidon
H2462.detail: Helba was a small city located in the territory of Asher, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. It was probably situated in the coastal region of Phoenicia, not far from Sidon. According to the account in Judges, the Asherites failed to drive out the Canaanite inhabitants (Judges 1:31).
H2462.origine: The name Helba means "fertile" in Hebrew, evoking the abundant lands of this coastal region. Although it is mentioned infrequently in Scripture, this city reflects the geography of the ancient Levant and the difficulty the Israelites had in fully conquering the promised land.
H2462.emploi: Helba appears only once in the Bible, in Judges 1:31, where it is listed among the cities from which the Asherites could not expel the original inhabitants. This mention is part of the account of the conquest: after the death of Joshua, the tribes of Israel did not completely subdue the Canaanite peoples in the territories assigned to them. Helba thus illustrates one of these pockets of pagan resistance in the land.

sens: City famous for its vineyards near Damascus
H2463.detail: Helbon is a small city located a few kilometers northwest of Damascus, Syria. It was renowned in antiquity for the exceptional quality of its grapes and wine, so much so that it appears in ancient texts as an important wine-producing center. The prophet Ezekiel specifically mentions it when he enumerates the luxury goods that Damascus trades with Tyre: the wine of Helbon is listed alongside white wool, thus attesting to its economic and commercial prestige in the ancient Near East (Ezekiel 27:18).
H2463.origine: The name Helbon likely means "fertile" in Hebrew, which perfectly suits a region known for the excellence of its wine production. The site still exists today under the modern Arabic name 'Helbon', in the Damascus region, and continues to be known for the quality of its grapes.
H2463.emploi: Helbon appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 27:18. The prophet describes the international trade of Tyre, one of the greatest merchant cities of the ancient world. He lists the cities and regions that supply the Tyrian markets with their specialized products: Judea and Israel bring wheat, honey, and oil; Helbon and Damascus provide the renowned wine and wool. This isolated but explicit mention testifies to the fame of Helbon's vineyards well beyond its local borders.

sens: Fragrant resin used in the worship of Israel
Ingredient of the sacred incense prescribed by God
H2464.detail:
1. Fragrant is a resin or aromatic gum, yellowish in color, that produces a strong and sweet smell when burned. It is a natural substance, probably originating from Persia or Syria, well known to ancient peoples. In Exodus 30:34, Moses is instructed to mix it with other aromatics: stacte, onyx, and pure incense, in equal parts, to make the incense for the altar of the tabernacle. 
2. As an ingredient of this sacred incense, fragrant was used in the most important utensils of Israel's worship: it was burned continuously on the altar of incense, at the heart of the sanctuary. This was an act of regular worship prescribed by God Himself, demonstrating the consecration of God's people.
H2464.origine: The Hebrew word חֶלְבְּנָה (chelbena) designates this gum-resin known in French as galbanum, named after the Greek term for the product. Hebrew likely borrows from an Eastern origin word, designating a substance known in the ancient Near East. The word appears only once in the Bible, in Exodus 30:34, during the prescription of the sacred incense.
H2464.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Exodus 30:34, where God lists the five ingredients of the incense that was to be prepared for the altar of the tabernacle: stacte, onyx, galbanum, pure incense, and salt. Each was to be included in equal measure, showing the importance of each component in this prescribed balance. This formula was reserved for the worship of God and prohibited for profane use (see Exodus 30:37-38).
H2464.portee: This word reminds us that worshiping God according to His law requires precision, order, and harmony. The ingredients of worship are not left to chance: God Himself establishes what should honor His presence in the sanctuary. The careful mixture of these aromatics symbolizes the unity and beauty of the prayer that the people raised to Him.

sens: The limited time of a human life, its duration
The inhabited world, the entirety of humans living on earth
The light of day, the brightness of the sun
H2465.detail: 1. The word primarily refers to the duration of a man's life, his existence in time. The psalmist says, "You have made my days a mere handbreadth; my life is nothing before you" (Psalm 39:6): our time on earth is infinitely short compared to God's eternity. This is why in Psalm 89:48, we ask God to remember "how fleeting is their life, that you have created all mankind" — we are but dust in the passing time. 2. By extension, the word refers to the inhabited world, the universe of living humans. In Psalm 17:14, the psalmist prays, "Deliver me from the men of this world": he speaks of the earthly domain, the place where unjust people enjoy their possessions. In Psalm 49:2, "Hear this, all you peoples... inhabitants of the world": it refers to the entirety of the inhabited earth, all humans. 3. Rarely, the word can simply mean the light of day: in Job 11:17, "Your days will be brighter than the noon day sun," where "sun" translates this same Hebrew word, referring to light and brightness.
H2465.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of thinness, lightness, or that which flows like a swift current. This image of fluidity and brevity perfectly suits human life: it flows and disappears. The word is mainly used in biblical poetry, particularly in the Psalms and wisdom literature, where the authors meditate on time and the vanity of human things.
H2465.emploi: The word appears 5 times in biblical Hebrew, concentrated in the Psalms and Job, books of wisdom and lamentation. The predominant meaning is that of time and limited human life, particularly developed in Psalms 39:6 and 89:48, where the poet measures his existence against the backdrop of divine eternity. The meaning of "world" (the entirety of humans or the inhabited earth) clearly appears in Psalms 17:14 and 49:2, where it designates the domain of the living and the unjust. The word can also evoke the light of day, as in Job 11:17. Its usage reveals a biblical vision: earthly life is brief and fragile, and the world of humans is a temporary spectacle in the eyes of the eternal Creator.
H2465.portee: This word invites the believer to sobriety in the face of life's brevity. It puts our earthly existence in its proper place: not eternal, but limited, and therefore to be lived with wisdom and fear of God. It also reminds us that the "world" — the order of humans with its injustices and fleeting pleasures — is not our true home: we are travelers, and God alone is eternal. It is an invitation to seek what endures beyond time.

sens: An elite warrior in the service of King David
A man from Nethopha
Son of Baana
H2466.detail:
1. Heled was one of the most powerful and loyal warriors of King David, chosen from among the best fighters in Israel. He is mentioned in the list of David's "thirty" or "mighty men," these exceptional men who formed the core of his army (1 Chronicles 11:30).
2. Heled came from Nethopha, a small town near Jerusalem. This geographical detail was important for precisely identifying the warriors in the official lists of the kingdom.
3. He was the son of Baana, also a warrior, which shows that certain families distinguished themselves by their courage and dedication to royal service.
H2466.origine: The name Heled (or its variant Heldai) means "one who passes quickly" or "transient," possibly evoking agility in battle. This name reflects the importance that the Hebrews attached to the qualities of a warrior: liveliness and responsiveness. The name appears in two forms, Heled and Heleb (or Heldai), which shows the common spelling variations in ancient Hebrew texts.
H2466.emploi: Heled appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:30. He is listed among the "mighty men of David," these renowned warriors who marked the reigns of Saul, David, and Solomon. This brief mention is enough to place him among the most esteemed men of his time, those whom King David held in high regard and associated with the defense and glory of the kingdom of Israel.
H2466.portee: The mention of Heled reminds us that the history of God's people was also built on the courage and faithfulness of ordinary people, whose names have been preserved to honor their dedication. These "mighty men" show that serving God and the king with excellence, in the domain that God entrusts to us, is a calling of great value.

sens: small burrowing animal
unclean animal according to the Law of Moses
H2467.detail:
1. The mole is a small burrowing animal that lives underground by digging tunnels. The Hebrew word likely refers to this well-known animal in the Middle East, or perhaps a now-extinct creature resembling the mole. It is an animal that crawls or moves underground.
2. In the Law given to Israel, the mole is listed among the unclean animals that the Israelites were not to eat. In Leviticus 11:29, it is enumerated with the mouse and the lizard in the list of small creeping creatures considered unclean, making it a taboo animal for the diet of God's people.
H2467.origine: The Hebrew word chôled designates a burrowing animal, probably linked to a root that evokes the idea of digging or moving underground. The exact term may have changed in reference over time, as the animal that ancient Israelites called this may no longer be accurately identified today. It belongs to the simple and concrete vocabulary of daily life in the Old Testament.
H2467.emploi: The word appears only once in the entire Hebrew Bible, in Leviticus 11:29. It is included in the list of animals that God declares unclean for Israel's consumption. This unique appearance makes it a rare term, likely referring to a small animal that is uncommon or unnoticed, but well-known enough to be mentioned in the dietary code of the Law.
H2467.portee: This small word reminds us of the concrete reality of the Law of Moses: it was concerned not only with grand issues but also with the details of daily life, including what was permitted or forbidden to eat. These laws about unclean animals taught Israel about holiness: being set apart for God means paying attention to every act, even the simplest ones like eating.

sens: Prophetess of the kingdom of Judah during the reign of King Josiah
H2468.detail: Hulda is a prophetess who lived in the kingdom of Judah during the reign of King Josiah (around 640-609 B.C.). When the priest Hilkiah discovered the book of the Law in the Temple, King Josiah consulted Hulda to know God's will regarding this sacred text found. She lived in Jerusalem, in the Mishneh district, and was married to Shallum. It was through her that God revealed His judgment on the kingdom and the king's responsibility regarding the rediscovered Law (2 Kings 22:14; 2 Chronicles 34:22).
H2468.origine: Her name means "weasel" in Hebrew, but her significance lies in her role as a spokesperson for God. She is one of the prophetesses of the Old Testament — like Deborah, Esther, and the mother of Samson — who receive and proclaim the divine word with authority in decisive moments of Israel's history.
H2468.emploi: Hulda appears only twice in the Bible, both times at the moment of the discovery of the book of the Law in the Temple under Josiah: in 2 Kings 22:14 and in 2 Chronicles 34:22. These two passages recount how the Temple officials and the king himself sought her prophetic counsel, recognizing her spiritual authority. Her consultation shows that even kings could turn to prophetesses to discern God's word.
H2468.portee: Hulda reminds us that God speaks through women as well as men, and that prophetic legitimacy comes from God, not from social status. Her role underscores the critical importance of rediscovery and obedience to the Word of God.

sens: military officer of King David
captain of the temple service
H2469G.detail: Heldaï is the name of a man who appears in biblical history at two different times. According to the source definition, he could refer on one hand to one of the mighty warriors of King David and the twelfth chief of the monthly divisions responsible for the temple service — a prestigious role in the religious organization of Israel. On the other hand, Heldaï is also the name of an exile who returned from Babylon during the time of Zechariah, mentioned in Zechariah 6:10, where he brings gold and silver offerings to the prophet Zechariah for the construction of the temple.
H2469G.origine: The name Heldaï means "worldly" or "carnal" in Hebrew. It comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the earthly world or worldly affairs. The Segond also mentions a namesake called Helem (חֵלֶם) in Zechariah 6:14, indicating that there may be a variant of this same name in the textual tradition.
H2469G.emploi: Heldaï appears once in the Segond 1910, in Zechariah 6:10, where he is named among the three men who return from Babylonian exile with precious offerings. Along with Tobijah and Jedaiah, he presents himself to Josiah, son of Zephaniah, and entrusts the prophet with the gold and silver intended for the crown of the high priest. This usage situates Heldaï in the period of the return from exile, a key moment of restoration for the worship and people of Israel. The presence of his name among the renowned religious leaders and exiles indicates his status as an important figure in Israel's history.

sens: One of the mighty warriors of King David
The twelfth military chief responsible for the administration of the temple
H2469H.detail:
1. Heldaï is one of David's renowned warriors, son of Baanah. He appears in the lists of the "mighty men" of the king, that is, the soldiers who distinguished themselves by their bravery and loyalty during the battles of King David's time.
2. He is the twelfth military chief responsible for organizing the temple service during the twelfth month of the year (1 Chronicles 27:15). In this capacity, he oversees a division of twenty-four thousand men tasked with the temple service.
H2469H.origine: The name Heldaï means "worldly" or "of the earthly world," perhaps reflecting a personal characteristic. This character is also referred to by the names Heled and Heleb in other biblical passages, variants that likely refer to the same person. His father Baanah was himself a respected warrior of David.
H2469H.emploi: Heldaï appears only once in the French translation of the Bible (1 Chronicles 27:15), where he is cited as the twelfth captain of the monthly temple service under King David, commanding a significant division. The source also indicates that he is mentioned in 2 Samuel 23:29, probably under the name Heled or Heleb, confirming his role as an elite warrior among the king's companions in arms.

sens: To lose physical strength, bodily vigor
To be ill, to suffer from a disease or infirmity
To be exhausted, fatigued by effort
To be downcast, discouraged in spirit
To be rendered infirm, injured or diminished
H2470A.detail:
1. To lose physical strength means becoming incapable of accomplishing what one used to do. Samson explains to Delilah that if he is shaved, his strength will leave him and he will become weak like any other man (Judges 16:17). The image is that of an athlete losing his energy and muscular power.

2. To be ill means to be affected by a disease or to suffer physically. The word can designate the state of one who is struck by illness and can no longer function normally.

3. To be exhausted means to become weary after hard work or prolonged effort. Isaiah describes the people who walk so much that they become tired (Isaiah 57:10), gradually losing their energy.

4. To be downcast emotionally means to lose one's courage and morale. Isaiah 14:10 speaks of one who has no inner strength in the face of his fate, becoming like all those who have fallen.

5. To be rendered infirm or diminished can come from an external action: God can cause the shepherd to make the sick sheep weak (Ezekiel 34:4, 34:16), meaning he weakens them instead of healing them.
H2470A.origine: The root חָלָה (cha.lah) expresses the fundamental idea of loss of vigor and weakening. It can be used in several grammatical modes (simple, intensive, causative) to mark different degrees: to be weak oneself, to become weak, or to make someone weak. The word evokes the image of a body losing its spring, of energy flowing away. Related words in Hebrew suggest wear and deterioration.
H2470A.emploi: This verb appears about 10 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the historical books (Judges) and prophetic books (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel). In the accounts of Samson (Judges 16:7, 11, 17), it describes the physical weakening caused by the breaking of the Nazarite vow. In the prophetic texts, it broadens its meaning: in Isaiah and Jeremiah, it designates the exhaustion of the people due to fruitless labor or incessant walking. In Ezekiel, it depicts the action of the shepherd (the king or God) towards the sheep: a weak sheep is one that has remained without help. The context determines whether the emphasis is on physical weakening, exhaustion, or moral discouragement.
H2470A.portee: This word reminds us that weakness is not a shame; it is part of the human condition. In the story of Samson, it shows that even one who has received extraordinary strength remains vulnerable to his own weaknesses. For the Christian, this term invites recognition of one's limits and seeking in God the strength that is lacking. The prophetic texts also suggest that God notices those who are weak and abandoned: He cares for the sheep that falter.

sens: To address a pressing prayer, a humble and insistent request to someone, especially to God
To beg someone to grant a favor, seeking to obtain their goodwill through sweet words
To flatter, cajole to obtain something from someone
H2470B.detail: 1. To implore God is to address Him with a prayer of urgency and humility, recognizing one's dependence and hoping for His intervention. Moses "implores" the Lord after the people's rebellion with the golden calf, presenting reasons for the Lord to relent from His anger (Exodus 32:11); similarly, King Asa "implores" the Lord in distress of war (2 Kings 13:4), and Manasseh "implores" the Lord when he is captive (2 Chronicles 33:12). 2. To implore someone is also to seek their favor or goodwill through sweet words or urgent efforts. The wealthy of the people "seek the favor" of the daughter of Tyre with gifts (Psalms 45:13), and many "flatter" the generous man to obtain his largesse (Proverbs 19:6). 3. This verb can therefore express prayer, intercession, or supplication before the Lord, but also the attempt to obtain something from a powerful person through kind words.
H2470B.origine: The Hebrew verb cha.lah has a root that first evokes the idea of making sweet, softening, or appeasing. The basic image is that of someone trying to soften another person's heart through their words or attitude. In the Piel form (intensive form of Hebrew), the verb expresses this action forcefully: to actively implore, to insistently beg. The Psalms and prophetic books use this word to describe the prayer of the believer or the people turning to God in need.
H2470B.emploi: This verb appears 15 times in the Old Testament, mainly in historical narratives, the Psalms, and wisdom literature. It primarily denotes prayer addressed to God in times of crisis: Moses imploring the Lord to spare Israel (Exodus 32:11), kings in military or personal distress imploring divine help (1 Kings 13:6; 2 Chronicles 33:12). The word is also used to describe supplication addressed to powerful men: seeking the favor of a king (Psalms 45:13), flattering a generous person to obtain their gifts (Proverbs 19:6). In the Psalms, the verb expresses the attitude of the believer who "implores" humbly for divine mercy (Psalms 119:58). The common nuance is always that of a humble and pressing approach to obtain something from someone more powerful.
H2470B.portee: This word teaches the believer that prayer is not a right but a humble and confident request addressed to the One who can do all. It reminds us that, before God or before men, we depend on the goodwill of others and that this dependence invites us to humility. This is especially true in prayer: the believer "implores" God not to force Him, but to acknowledge their need and place themselves under the authority of the Lord. At the same time, the word shows that God sincerely listens to the supplications of His people and acts in response.

sens: To suffer from an illness or physical infirmity
To be injured or weakened by a wound
To experience deep sadness or grief
To become weak or exhausted
H2470H.detail:
1. To be afflicted with an illness or to suffer physically: the word describes the state of one who is struck by illness and cannot rise or carry out their activities. Jacob is ill (Genesis 48:1), Hezekiah is gravely ill (Isaiah 38:1), and Ahaziah, injured after his fall, asks if he will recover (2 Kings 1:2).
2. To be injured or weakened as a result of a wound: the word applies to one who has received a blow or wound and bears its consequences. The king of Israel cries, "I am wounded" after being struck in battle and cannot remain on the battlefield (2 Chronicles 18:33).
3. To suffer from moral pain, sadness, or unfulfilled desire that weighs on the heart: the word can express inner affliction. A disappointed hope "makes the heart sick" (Proverbs 13:12), and the lover suffers from absence: "I am sick with love" (Song of Solomon 5:8).
4. To become weak, to weaken or exhaust: the word can describe a general exhaustion of the body or spirit after effort or trial. Daniel "felt ill" after having the vision (Daniel 8:27).
H2470H.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of weakness and lack of strength. It primarily denotes a physical state — that of an weakened body — and extends to any form of deterioration, whether it be an injury, an illness, or emotional exhaustion. The root appears in several verbal forms in Hebrew, each slightly nuanced in meaning: the illness one suffers, that one feels coming, or that one brings upon oneself.
H2470H.emploi: The word appears 38 times in the Old Testament, mainly in historical narratives and poems. It is used to describe the illness of important characters — Jacob, Hezekiah, Ahab — and also appears in the laws of Deuteronomy 29:22, where God speaks of the evils He sends upon those who reject Him. The wisdom books use it figuratively: the sick heart of one who hopes in vain (Proverbs 13:12), or the lover sick with love (Song of Solomon 5:8). Isaiah and the Kings frequently use it to show how illness tests the king and drives him to seek God's help.
H2470H.portee: This word reminds us that illness, in the Bible, is not a mere medical event but a reality that affects the whole being — body, heart, soul. It reveals our fragility and often drives us to cry out to God. Sick Hezekiah finds confidence in God; the lover in the Song knows that only the one she loves can heal her. For the Christian reader, this word invites us to see in illness an opportunity to depend more on God and to recognize our human limits.

sens: To be physically weak or ill
To suffer morally, to be afflicted or saddened
To feel pain or anguish
To be injured or struck by a wound
H2470I.detail:
1. The verb primarily describes the physical state of one who loses their strength: to be ill, weak, diminished. In Isaiah 53:10, the suffering servant "will be ill" while fulfilling the divine plan.
2. The word extends to inner suffering: to be saddened, afflicted, to grieve. In Amos 6:6, those who do not "grieve" over the ruin of Joseph refuse to empathize with the misfortune of others.
3. Physical and moral anguish are intertwined: the woman in labor in Jeremiah 4:31 gives "cries of anguish," the pain of childbirth embodying agony.
4. The term can denote a serious wound, a plague that deeply affects. In Jeremiah 14:17, the daughter of Zion has been struck by a "very painful plague" that causes the prophet's tears to flow incessantly.
H2470I.origine: The Hebrew verb חָלָה comes from a root evoking weakness, weakening, as if vitality were flowing out of the body or soul. The family of the word includes terms for illness, fatigue, pain. The basic image is that of a force collapsing, whether it be physical (illness) or moral (grief), as in Hebrew the body and soul are not sharply separated.
H2470I.emploi: This verb appears twelve times in the Old Testament, spread across historical, prophetic, and wisdom books. It describes either a real illness (Isaiah 53:10) or an emotional state of affliction, grief, or refusal to empathize (Amos 6:6). In Ecclesiastes 5:12, wealth accumulated in the wrong place becomes a "serious evil." In Jeremiah, the prophet uses the word to express his compassion for the people's wounds (14:17) and the pains of childbirth as an image of national turmoil (4:31). The meaning thus oscillates between physical illness and moral suffering, illustrating how Israel feels misfortune as a wound of the heart as much as of the body.
H2470I.portee: This word invites the reader to recognize that illness, weakness, and pain are unvarnished biblical realities: God does not hide them, and His prophets express them candidly. But the verb also reminds us that empathizing with the suffering of others — instead of ignoring it — is an act of justice and love. Finally, seeing the suffering Servant as "ill" for our sins (Isaiah 53:10) gives meaning to all pain: it is never absurd for one who hopes in Christ.

sens: Flat and thin bread, baked, intended to be presented before God
Offering or portion of bread consecrated in the Temple worship
Leavened or unleavened bread, soaked in oil, serving as food or gift
H2471.detail:
1. The cake is a fine, flat bread, baked in the oven, that the Israelites prepared with fine flour, oil, and often without leaven. It was a more refined form of bread than ordinary bread, intended for worship: in Exodus 29:2, it refers to unleavened cakes kneaded with oil, prepared for the consecration of Aaron and his sons.
2. In sacrifices and offerings, the cake had a religious significance: it was an offering presented before the Lord. In Leviticus 7:12-13, cakes accompany the thank offering, and leavened bread is even added to the offering, which shows the variety of forms used according to the type of sacrifice.
3. The cake could be drizzled with oil, soaked in oil, or even fried: in Leviticus 7:12, there are cakes "of fried fine flour and kneaded with oil." It was both a cultic and festive food, also shared between the priest and the one who brought the offering, as shown in 2 Samuel 6:19 where David distributes cakes to everyone during the procession of the Ark.
H2471.origine: The Hebrew word חַלָּה (challah) literally means a flat and fine bread. Its etymology suggests the idea of something pierced or perforated, perhaps in reference to the holes or marks left on the surface of the baked bread. This word applies to breads of various shapes in the sacred cuisine of the Temple, always prepared with care and good ingredients.
H2471.emploi: The word appears 11 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the sacrificial codes of Leviticus, but also in Exodus and Numbers. It refers to specific breads of worship: unleavened presentation breads in Exodus 29:2 and 29:23, portions offered in sacrifices in Leviticus 2:4, 7:12-13 and 8:26, nazirite vow breads in Numbers 6:15 and 6:19, and the offering portion in Numbers 15:20. There is only one occurrence outside the strict cultic context: in 2 Samuel 6:19, David distributes cakes to the people during a religious feast, showing that the term also applies to festive breads that are consecrated.
H2471.portee: The cake reminds the believer of the place of refined food and offering in the relationship with God. It is not ordinary bread, but bread of quality and care, presented to God or distributed in His name. It is an invitation to understand that the worship of the God of Israel required the best, and that religious fellowship was also manifested through the sharing of blessed food.

sens: Night vision that occurs during sleep
Message or revelation that God communicates through the dream
Product of the imagination that can be deceptive or vain
H2472.detail:
1. A dream is a vision that appears to someone during their sleep, natural and spontaneous (Genesis 20:3: "God appeared in a dream to Abimelech during the night"). It is an ordinary experience of sleep, where images and thoughts pass through the mind.

2. In the Bible, God often uses dreams as a means of revelation and communication (Numbers 12:6: "I will speak to him in a dream"). The dream then becomes a prophetic channel, carrying a divine message that must be interpreted carefully (Genesis 41:11: each one "received an explanation related to the dream he had").

3. A dream can also be vain or deceptive, a mere fiction of the sleeping mind, without value or substance (Jeremiah 23:28: "Why mix straw with wheat?" — false dreams are not worth the word of God). The Bible warns against those who claim to interpret dreams without divine authority.
H2472.origine: The Hebrew word חֲלוֹם (halôm) comes from a root that refers to the idea of "seeing" or "perceiving" in the darkness of sleep. In Aramaic, a similar form (chelèm) is found. Dreams occupy an important place in biblical narratives, especially in the stories of Joseph and Daniel, where God reveals Himself through symbolic images.
H2472.emploi: The word "dream" appears 55 times in the Old Testament, especially in Genesis (stories of Joseph, Abimelech, Pharaoh), in Numbers, and in Jeremiah. Biblical dreams are divided into two categories: ordinary dreams (Genesis 37:5-10, where Joseph recounts his dreams to his family) and prophetic or divine dreams (1 Kings 3:5, where God speaks to Solomon; Numbers 12:6). Jeremiah warns against false prophets who invoke lying dreams (Jeremiah 23:27-28). Daniel receives visions in dreams (Daniel 2:1-3), often complex and full of symbolism requiring interpretation.
H2472.portee: The dream reminds the reader that God is not limited to ordinary communications: He can reveal Himself in the rest and vulnerability of sleep. This invites spiritual vigilance — to discern between vain dreams and true messages from God — and trust: our nights are not beyond the Lord's reach. It is an invitation to listen to God in all moments of our lives.

sens: city in the mountains of Judah
locality given to the Levitical priests
H2473G.detail: Holon is a small city located in the mountains of the region of Judah. Its name means "sandy," possibly evoking sandy or stony terrain. This city was assigned to the priests of the tribe of Levi as one of their cities of residence, in accordance with the organization of the territory after the conquest (Joshua 21:15). It is mentioned in the list of cities of Judah (Joshua 15:51) and in the list of Levitical cities.
H2473G.origine: The name Holon comes from the Hebrew חוֹל (ḥol), which means "sand" or "sandy terrain." It is a descriptive geographical name, common in ancient Israel, that characterizes the soil or landscape of the place. The name reflects the topography of the region of the mountains of Judah.
H2473G.emploi: Holon appears only twice in the Bible, both times in the book of Joshua. It first appears in the list of cities of the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:51), where it is listed among the eleven cities of the district of Goshen. It then reappears in the list of the forty-eight cities assigned to the Levites for their habitation and pastures (Joshua 21:15). The text specifies that each Levitical city had a "suburb," meaning surrounding common lands reserved for livestock grazing. This double mention shows that Holon belonged to Judah but also welcomed priests and Levites.

sens: City in the land of Moab
H2473H.detail: Holon is a city located in Moab, a region of Transjordan east of the Dead Sea. It appears in a prophecy against the Moabite peoples: the prophet Jeremiah announces that God's judgment falls upon the Moabite cities, including Holon (Jeremiah 48:21).
H2473H.origine: The name Holon may derive from a root meaning "sand," which would evoke the desert geography of the Moabite region. Its precise etymology remains uncertain, but it likely reflects characteristics of the local terrain.
H2473H.emploi: Holon appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 48:21. It is listed among the Moabite cities that are subject to divine judgment. This mention places Holon within the general prophecy against Moab, without specific details about its importance or history.

sens: Opening in the wall of a building, to let in light and air
Means of observing or looking outside without being seen
Means of access beyond a barrier or enclosure
H2474.detail:
1. A window is an opening made in the wall of a structure to illuminate and ventilate the interior. It is the opening itself that defines the word, with its edges in stone or wood. In Noah's ark, he opens "the window that he had made" to let out the raven (Genesis 8:6); the windows of the temple are "strongly barred" for security reasons (1 Kings 6:4).
2. The window allows one to see what is happening outside or at the neighbor's. Michal looks through the window and sees King David dancing (1 Chronicles 15:29); the woman of Proverbs sits by the window to observe the young men passing by (Proverbs 7:6).
3. The opening can serve as a passage for entering or exiting, bypassing the door or wall. Rahab helps the spies escape through the window by lowering them with a rope (Joshua 2:15,18,21); similarly, Saul escapes from David by being let down through the window (1 Samuel 19:12).
H2474.origine: The Hebrew word חַלּוֹן (challon) comes from a root meaning "to pierce" or "to dig." This word literally describes the result of the action: a hole pierced in the wall. It exists only in biblical Hebrew and Aramaic to denote this concrete reality of the ancient house. The windows of ancient Eastern homes were often small and high, sometimes equipped with grilles or bars, hence the image of the deliberate piercing of the wall.
H2474.emploi: This word appears 27 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the historical books (Kings, Samuel, Chronicles), Wisdom (Proverbs), the Prophets (Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Joel, Zephaniah), and one poem (Song of Songs). It primarily designates the window as a simple architectural opening in buildings: the ark, the temple, fortresses, and private homes. But the Bible also uses it figuratively as a point of observation or surveillance: to look, to spy, to escape. In Ezekiel, who describes the future temple in detail, windows appear repeatedly, structuring his visionary architecture (Ezekiel 40-41). The word finally carries a nuance of urgency or clandestineness when it becomes a means of escape: it is through the window that one quickly escapes, without going through the main entrance.
H2474.portee: Understanding what a window represents in the Bible reminds us that Scripture speaks first of the concrete and the everyday: houses, walls, light entering the room. It helps us imagine life in biblical times. But more profoundly, windows symbolize in the Bible an opening to the world: they allow us to see what eludes us, to communicate, to flee. It is also through the windows that Ezekiel receives his vision of the new temple, which becomes symbolically the heart of divine restoration.

sens: abandoned or defenseless person
one who is left to ruin or death
H2475.detail:
1. A forsaken person is someone forgotten, without protection, to whom no one comes to help. The image is of a man alone, to whom others have turned their backs. In Proverbs 31:8, the wise man exhorts to "open your mouth for the mute, for the cause of all the forsaken": those whose cries no one hears, those whom society has cast aside.
2. In a more serious sense, it refers to one destined for destruction or death: a human being whose fate seems sealed, abandoned to misfortune. The word evokes both abandonment and the end that results from it.
H2475.origine: The Hebrew word חֲלוֹף (cha.loph) comes from a root that means "to pass," "to disappear," "to exchange." A forsaken person is literally one who "passes," who disappears from sight and memory, someone for whom no time is taken. The root also evokes the idea of replacement or change: one is exchanged for another, replaced by someone more useful. This gives the word a shade of social contempt.
H2475.emploi: This word appears only once in the Greek New Testament (it refers here to the Hebrew Old Testament). In Proverbs 31:8, it designates the unfortunate whom wealth and power forget: the mute who cannot plead his cause, the poor, the widows, all those whom the social system crushes. The context of Proverbs makes it a moral figure: it calls upon those who have the power of speech (and power in general) to defend not their friends or peers, but precisely those whom no one defends. It is an exhortation to social justice.
H2475.portee: This word reminds the reader that they have a responsibility toward the most vulnerable. From a Christian perspective, it calls to recognize and assist those who are rejected or forgotten, and to see in them a creature made in the image of God, not a person of little value. It is a call to active compassion and justice.

sens: State of being defeated or overcome in battle
Lack of physical or moral strength
Failure, collapse
H2476.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the state of one who has lost the battle, who is defeated and crushed by the enemy. In Exodus 32:18, Moses hears noise at the foot of Sinai and asks Aaron what is happening: "It is neither the cry of victors nor the cry of the defeated" — he instinctively understands that "defeated" means the rout, the cry of the vanquished.
2. More broadly, the word expresses any lack of strength: the weakening of the body, exhaustion after effort, or moral impotence in the face of a trial.
3. It can also describe a prostration, a complete collapse — the state of one who can no longer rise or resist.
H2476.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of softness, relaxation (like a muscle that loses its tension). It is the opposite of strength and rigidity. The feminine form we have here reinforces the idea of a quality, a passive and involuntary state: it is not a simple temporary fatigue, but a condition of powerlessness.
H2476.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Exodus 32:18. Moses, descending from Sinai with the tablets of the law, hears noise in the camp — it is the people worshiping the golden calf. Joshua tells him that he hears "a cry of war," but Moses corrects him: it is not the voice of victory, nor that of military defeat, it is simply the sound of singing. The word "defeated" (weakness) illustrates here the characteristic noise of a crushed army, in contrast to the noise of a triumphant army.
H2476.portee: This word reminds us that weakness, defeat, and powerlessness are realities that God knows and that the Bible does not hide. It also shows that true strength does not come from us, but from God alone: understanding our weakness is the path to turning to Him and seeking His strength.

sens: Region or city in Mesopotamia where the Assyrians deported the Israelite captives
H2477.detail: Chalach is a region or city in Mesopotamia (ancient Iraq) that was under the control of the Assyrian empire. It is where the king of Assyria forced the Israelites to settle after the fall of the Northern Kingdom. In 2 Kings 17:6, during the capture of Samaria by the king of Assyria, the Israelite captives are "carried away to Assyria" and "settled in Chalach, and by the river Chabor, and in the cities of the Medes." This place symbolizes the exile and dispersion of the people of Israel, separated from their promised land. The three biblical mentions (2 Kings 17:6, 18:11, and 1 Chronicles 5:26) all describe massive deportations to this same location: first the Northern Kingdom, then the Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh.
H2477.origine: The name Chalach comes from the Hebrew חֲלַח and literally means "painful" or "suffering." This etymology reflects the tragic nature of this place: it is never mentioned in the Bible except as a destination of exile and captivity, never as a land of blessing or freedom. The name carries the reality of deportation within it.
H2477.emploi: Chalach appears three times in the Bible, exclusively in the accounts of the deportation of the Northern Kingdom of Israel. It is always mentioned alongside other places of captivity: the river Chabor (or Khabur), Gozan, and the cities of the Medes. These three biblical references (2 Kings 17:6, 18:11, and 1 Chronicles 5:26) recount how different Israelite groups — first the population of Samaria, then the eastern tribes — were deported to Assyria. The mention in 1 Chronicles 5:26 adds that these captives "have remained until this day," suggesting a definitive separation and the absence of return to the promised land for the Northern Kingdom.
H2477.portee: The fate of those taken to Chalach reminds the Christian reader of the consequence of collective unfaithfulness and turning away from the true God. But this passage also speaks of the sovereign action of the Lord: even in exile, even under foreign domination, God does not lose sight of His people. This deportation remains a call to repentance and a lesson on the seriousness of straying from the God of the covenant.

sens: City of Judah, built on a hill
H2478.detail: Halhul is a small town in the mountainous territory of Judah, located near Hebron on the road leading south from Jerusalem. It appears in the list of cities assigned to the tribe of Judah after the conquest of Canaan (Joshua 15:58).
H2478.origine: The name Halhul means "trembling" in Hebrew, likely referring to an earthquake or a remarkable geographical event of the place. It is a typical Semitic toponym of the mountainous regions of Judah.
H2478.emploi: Halhul is mentioned only once in the Bible, in the book of Joshua (15:58), where it is listed among the cities of the territory of Judah after the land distribution among the tribes of Israel. It is part of a group of small mountain localities in Judah, alongside Beth-Zur and Gedor.

sens: Intense physical pain and body tremors
Terror that overwhelms the mind and paralyzes
Deep disturbance and inner turmoil in the face of danger
H2479.detail:
1. The word first describes raw physical suffering: sharp pains, convulsions, involuntary body tremors. In Isaiah 21:3, the prophet speaks of "pangs" and "spasms" that assail him like a woman in labor — an image of contraction and physical paroxysm.
2. It also designates the terror that seizes the soul, paralyzing will and judgment. In Ezekiel 30:4 and 30:9, "dismay" falls upon Ethiopia: it is the panic in the face of disaster when the threat becomes certain and inevitable.
3. More broadly, it expresses a total collapse — physical and moral — in the face of the abyss: knees that tremble, loins that suffer, faces that pale (Nahum 2:11). Anguish is not a mere emotion; it is a dissolution of the whole being.
H2479.origine: The word comes from a root that expresses the idea of contracting, trembling, swirling. It is linked to the image of pain that twists the body and fear that paralyzes it. In biblical Hebrew, this word belongs to the family of terms that describe the spasmodic and involuntary movements of the body in distress — a very physical, very concrete root.
H2479.emploi: This word appears 4 times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the prophets (Isaiah, Ezekiel, Nahum) to describe moments of extreme crisis. It designates either the personal suffering of the prophet in the face of the vision of divine judgment (Isaiah 21:3), or the collective terror that seizes a people before punishment (Ezekiel 30:4, 30:9), or the physical debacle of warriors before the enemy (Nahum 2:11). The word thus oscillates between organic pain and existential fear, but always with this charge of total helplessness.
H2479.portee: This word reminds us that biblical anguish is never superficial: it affects the whole body and reveals an ignored truth — that of divine judgment or mortal fragility. For the Christian reader, it also sheds light on the price of redemption: only the peace of Christ can free from this anguish that knots the heart and body.

sens: quickly grasp what is said
accept a word as true
confirm by acceptance what has just been heard
H2480.detail:
1. To take at face value means to immediately and quickly grasp a word, a statement, or a proposition. It is like catching a ball in mid-air: one instantly captures what has just been said. In 1 Kings 20:33, the men of Ben-Hadad hear Ahab call their king "brother" and they "take him at his word" — they seize this word and accept it as a declaration of sincere alliance.
2. To take at face value also means to accept a statement as true and rely on it. It is not to discuss, hesitate, or verify: it is to believe and act immediately. The servants of Ben-Hadad take Ahab's word literally and immediately conclude that a brotherly friendship has just been born.
3. By extension, it is to confirm by one's adherence what has just been heard: by accepting the word, one makes it effective, one concretizes it. The servants transform a word into action by rushing to bring their king to Ahab.
H2480.origine: The Hebrew verb חָלַט (halat) primarily means "to catch" or "to seize" — the image is that of a rapid and decisive capture, as one catches an object that is flying or escaping. In Hiphil (intensive-causative form), it takes on the meaning of "to make seize" or "to take." The verb expresses the idea of capturing a word: one captures it and seizes it as true, without delay.
H2480.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 1 Kings 20:33. It describes the reaction of the servants of Ben-Hadad when they hear Ahab call them "brothers": they interpret this brotherly word as an offer of sincere alliance and, not wanting to let this opportunity pass, they "take him at his word" by accepting immediately and bringing their king to seal the agreement. The context shows an act of rapid trust, perhaps a bit naïve, in the face of a word that seems favorable.
H2480.portee: This word reminds us of the importance of our words: they can be "taken at face value," accepted as true, and engage those who hear them. For the believer, this invites weighing one's words with sincerity, for one never knows who will seize them to act. It is also a warning against credulity: accepting a word without scrutinizing it can lead to unpleasant surprises, as Ahab will discover.

sens: Precious object worn as decoration, notably a necklace or jewelry
Coordinated set of jewelry or matching ornaments
Ornamental beauty, elegance of what is crafted with art
H2481.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a valuable object intended to adorn the body: a necklace, a piece of jewelry. In Proverbs 25:12, a "fine gold ornament" (שׁלבנבול) evokes something precious and beautiful, placed next to a gold ring to illustrate the splendor of a wise word that corrects.
2. The word can also refer to a beautiful shape, a graceful silhouette, particularly when it recalls the art of the jeweler. In Song of Solomon 7:2, the contours of the beloved's hip are compared to "necklaces, the work of an artist's hands": it is less about the jewelry itself than about an elegant and delicate work, a beauty shaped.
3. More generally, it is the ornamentation, everything that beautifies and pleases the eye — the idea that something is pleasant to see because it has been cared for, crafted, as by an artist.
H2481.origine: The Hebrew word חֲלִי comes from a root meaning probably "to turn" or "to thread," related to the work of the artisan who shapes metal to make jewelry. It is from the same family as other words related to ornament and adornment. The initial concrete meaning of jewelry has extended to everything that adorns with grace and delicacy.
H2481.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Proverbs 25:12, it designates a fine gold ornament that symbolizes the beauty of wise correction — the idea is that the right word is precious and beautiful, like fine jewelry. In Song of Solomon 7:2, it describes the elegant forms of the beloved as they resemble artistically crafted necklaces: the ornament becomes an image of natural grace, delicacy visible in every detail of the body. In both cases, the word emphasizes the idea of beauty, finesse, and value.
H2481.portee: This word invites the reader to see the beauty of wisdom and that of the human body as precious creations, sculpted with care. In Proverbs, wise correction is comparable to fine jewelry — it is valuable because it enhances the one who receives it. In Song of Solomon, the body becomes an object of pure aesthetic admiration, celebrated for its delicate harmony. It is an invitation to recognize that true beauty bears the mark of work and care.

sens: City of Galilee located in the Promised Land
H2482.detail: Hali is a small city mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time of the land distribution among the tribes of Israel. It was located on the border of the territory of Asher, between two other localities: Helkath and Bethen (Joshua 19:25). It was one of the lesser-known cities, listed alongside others to precisely delineate the territorial boundaries of the tribe of Asher in Galilee.
H2482.origine: The Hebrew name חֲלִי (hali) literally means "necklace" or "ornament for the neck." The exact origin of this geographical name is not documented in the Scriptures, but it reflects a common practice: ancient localities in the Near East often bore names evoking objects, animals, or natural phenomena. This city, like many others in Galilee, was known to the Israelites without being a major center.
H2482.emploi: Hali appears only once in the entire Bible, in Joshua 19:25, during the listing of the border cities of Asher. It is included in the list enumerated by Joshua that determines the boundaries of the territory assigned to this tribe after the conquest of Canaan. Its unique appearance in this administrative context shows that it was a small locality serving as a landmark for the borders, without great historical or religious significance in the eyes of the biblical authors.

sens: Physical state of a person suffering from a bodily affliction
Intense physical pain or suffering
Chronic or serious condition that weakens
Evil, deterioration in a broad sense
State of the heart or soul tormented by guilt or affliction
H2483.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a true illness, a physical affliction. In Deuteronomy 7:15, God promises to remove diseases from the people, particularly those of Egypt. It is a reality of the human body subjected to illness.
2. The word emphasizes the painful and debilitating aspect: the illness of King Ben-Hadad was so severe that it was questioned whether he would recover (2 Kings 8:9). It brings intense physical suffering that affects all daily life.
3. In 2 Chronicles 21:15, the "illness of the bowels" described as worsening day by day shows a chronic and progressive evil, heralding a painful end of life.
4. Sometimes the word takes on a broader meaning: the illness of the psalmist (Psalms 41:4) includes the torment of the heart and spiritual trial, not just the body. It is a state of deep malaise.
5. In Isaiah (1:5), the "sick head" of the people symbolizes an entire nation that is corrupt and suffering, as if sin were a moral illness.
H2483.origine: The Hebrew word חֳלִי comes from the root חלה (hala), which means to be weak, to languish, to be ill. This root evokes the idea of softness, of weakening. The word belongs to the family of terms describing physical affliction: a sick person is someone whose strength abandons them. It is a concrete and bodily word, related to the suffering and weakening body.
H2483.emploi: This word appears 22 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the historical books (Kings, Chronicles) and prophetic books (Isaiah, Jeremiah). It describes sometimes a true illness of a person (1 Kings 17:17: the deadly illness of the widow's son), sometimes an affliction that strikes as divine punishment (2 Chronicles 21:15). It can also symbolize moral or spiritual evil: Isaiah uses it to describe the state of the sinful people ("the whole head is sick"). In Isaiah 53, the suffering servant bears not only our sins but also our illnesses, showing that healing is linked to atonement.
H2483.portee: This word reminds us that illness is a reality of the created world, inseparable from the sinful human condition. It can be punishment, but also an occasion for faith: the sick in Psalm 41 are supported by God on their bed of pain. For the believer, the word also opens the promise of healing in Christ, who bore our infirmities (Isaiah 53:4).

sens: Ornament worn around the neck, usually made of precious metal or beads
Luxury adornment that signifies wealth or social status
In a figurative sense, that which adorns or embellishes
That which enslaves or binds
H2484.detail: 1. A necklace is a piece of jewelry worn around the neck, often made of gold, silver, or adorned with precious stones. It is a personal decoration intended to beautify the wearer. In Hosea 2:15, the unfaithful woman adorns her body with necklaces before running after her lovers, showing how much she cares about her appearance. 2. The necklace is also a sign of wealth and status: wearing valuable necklaces indicates that one has the means to afford luxury adornments. Among ancient peoples, this distinguished the wearer. 3. The word can also metaphorically refer to anything that adorns or embellishes, such as grace or beauty that adorns a person. 4. In Hebrew, the word can also evoke that which chains or holds, like a noose around the neck — an image of servitude or captivity.
H2484.origine: The Hebrew word חֶלְיָה (chel.yah) belongs to the family of terms designating ornaments and body adornments. It derives from a root that evokes the idea of suspending or hanging around the neck. This type of jewelry was very common in ancient Mesopotamia and Egypt, where necklaces and chains marked social rank and wealth.
H2484.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Hosea 2:15. In this passage, the prophet describes the unfaithful woman of Israel (symbolizing the idolatrous people) who adorns herself with necklaces before going to worship the Baals. The context is one of divine rebuke: God reproaches Israel for its unfaithfulness and its pursuit of false gods, illustrated by all the luxury adornments she puts on to go to her idolatrous rendezvous. It is the only occurrence of the word in the preserved biblical texts.
H2484.portee: This passage invites the reader to see how the pursuit of luxury and appearance can divert us from faithfulness to God. The necklaces in Hosea symbolize pride and the seduction of false worship: one adorns oneself to follow idols. For the Christian, this reminds us that true beauty comes not from external adornments, but from a faithful relationship with God.

sens: wind musical instrument, tube pierced with holes
sound of the flute, melody
expression of joy and celebration
expression of lamentation and mourning
H2485.detail:
1. The flute is a wind musical instrument: a tube pierced with holes that is played with the fingers and mouth. In 1 Samuel 10:5, a group of prophets comes down from the high place "preceded by the lyre, the tambourine, the flute, and the harp," showing that the flute accompanies other instruments in processions and celebrations.
2. The word also refers to the sound or melody produced by this instrument. In Isaiah 30:29, the faithful walk "to the sound of the flute" toward the mountain of the Lord, as if the flute guides their joyful path.
3. The flute evokes joy and celebration: it enlivens festivities. In 1 Kings 1:40, "all the people went up after him, and the people played the flute and rejoiced greatly," celebrating the coronation of King Solomon.
4. Sometimes, the sound of the flute expresses lament and mourning. In Jeremiah 48:36, the prophet says, "my heart moans like a flute over Moab," comparing his lamentation to the plaintive sound of a flute, because the riches of Moab are lost. Thus, the same instrument can express two opposing emotions depending on the context.
H2485.origine: The Hebrew word חָלִיל comes from a root meaning "to pierce" or "to hollow out": the flute is indeed a tube that is pierced to make holes. The family of this word in Hebrew evokes everything that is hollowed out or excavated. This very ancient instrument was common in the ancient Near East and played an important role in the religious celebrations and mourning moments of the people of Israel.
H2485.emploi: The word חָלִיל appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, always in a context of music and celebration or lamentation. It accompanies significant moments: the coming of the prophets (1 Samuel 10:5), the coronation of a king (1 Kings 1:40), festive feasts (Isaiah 5:12), the ascent to the temple (Isaiah 30:29), or the expression of mourning (Jeremiah 48:36). It is a "social" instrument, played in groups or processions, never alone. In Isaiah 5:12, the flute is associated with feasts where God is forgotten: it then embodies human entertainment diverted from its true purpose.
H2485.portee: The flute reminds us that joy, music, and celebration are gifts from God. But it also warns us: a joy that turns its back on God, that "gives itself to celebration" while ignoring the work of the Lord, becomes empty. The flute can also express deep and legitimate pain in the face of loss: it is an invitation to weep with those who weep, for lamentation also has its place in the life of faith.

sens: Categorical expression of distance: strongly rejecting an idea, action, or thought
Call to God to keep away evil, guilt
Absolute refusal to commit an act deemed wrong or unworthy
H2486.detail:
1. It is an exclamation of horror or protest in the face of something contrary to justice or honor. The speaker forcefully rejects the idea of acting in such a way or that such a thing should happen. In Genesis 18:25, Abraham protests: "Far be it from you to do such a thing!" — he is indignant that God could put the righteous to death with the wicked.
2. It is also a cry to God: "God forbid!" or "May God preserve me!" It is used to implore His protection against sin or misfortune. In 1 Samuel 12:23, Samuel says: "Far be it from me to sin against the Lord" — he rejects the very idea of abandoning prayer for the people.
3. It is an irrevocable refusal: the speaker declares that he will never do such a thing, as it revolts him. In 1 Samuel 26:11, David asserts: "Far be it from me to lay a hand on the Lord's anointed" — it is a solemn oath of inviolable respect, even toward a king who pursues him.
H2486.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root expressing distance, remoteness, absence. It is a rare, intensive word that carries the idea of rejecting something very far away, putting it absolutely aside. Structurally, it is a fixed exclamation, often reinforced by repetition ("Far from you! far from you!") to amplify the rejection.
H2486.emploi: This word appears 19 times in the Old Testament, mainly among historical narrators and in Job. It always arises at the heart of a moral conflict or a serious decision. David and Samuel use it to affirm their faithfulness despite pressures. Abraham uses it to contest God Himself, should He act unjustly. Naboth cries it out to Ahab to refuse to renounce his ancestors (1 Kings 21:3). Job uses it to defend his integrity (Job 27:5, 34:10). In each occurrence, the word marks the moment when a character must choose: to submit to God and justice, or to yield to the pressure of the world. It is always a line that will not be crossed.
H2486.portee: For the Christian reader, this exclamation becomes a mirror: where are my "far from me"? What are the things against which I cry no? It teaches that faith is not measured by sweet words, but by courageous refusals in the face of evil. It also shows that one can cry out against God (like Abraham) and remain just, as long as one is driven by a love for justice. It is an invitation to cultivate convictions so strong that they escape from us like cries.

sens: Spare clothing, additional garment
Succession of elements that replace each other, alternation
Relief, replacement of people in a function
Relief, interruption of a painful situation
H2487.detail:
1. The most common concrete meaning: an additional garment that is changed when the first is dirty or worn out. Joseph gives his brothers "spare garments" (Genesis 45:22), and Samson promises "thirty spare garments" to whoever solves his riddle (Judges 14:12).
2. By extension, an organized alternation: the workers of Lebanon work "alternately," one month there and two months at home (1 Kings 5:14). This is a system of relief where groups succeed one another.
3. The relief of people assigned to a task: one group replaces another to continue the work, like those who take turns.
4. In a figurative and metaphorical sense, an interruption or relief: Job asks if after death there is a "replacement," a change of state that would bring respite (Job 14:14).
H2487.origine: This word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to change, to succeed one another." It describes the idea of alternating, moving from one thing to another. The same root produces the verb "to change" and the noun "change." The word evokes a movement of replacement, like when one changes from one garment to another or when one person replaces another in a job.
H2487.emploi: This word appears 11 times in biblical Hebrew, mostly in practical contexts: spare garments are a valuable gift (Genesis, Judges, 2 Kings), and they are also used figuratively for systems of alternation (1 Kings 5:14 with those who take turns). Some occurrences are more metaphorical: Job uses it to speak of relief or a change of state after death. In the Psalms and Job, the word takes on a more abstract hue, signifying variation or succession in the course of life.
H2487.portee: This word reminds us that God provides for material needs and that hospitality includes generous gifts. It also shows that work can be organized fairly, with reliefs to avoid exhaustion. On a spiritual level, the idea of "replacement" raises a question: is there a change or relief beyond death? This is a question that a believer can meditate on.

sens: clothing or armor taken from a defeated enemy
goods taken from the adversary in war
everything that has been forcibly taken from someone
H2488.detail:
1. In the most concrete sense, spoil is a garment or armor taken from an enemy in battle. In Judges 14:19, Samson kills thirty men and takes their spoils — these are their garments — which he gives as a reward to those who solved his riddle. It is an act of plundering by the victor over the vanquished.
2. More broadly, spoil refers to all the goods, wealth, or war equipment that one appropriates by defeating the enemy. In 2 Samuel 2:21, Abner invites Asahel to seize one of the young men and take his spoil: he speaks of the loot that can be taken in battle.
3. The word evokes everything that is torn away, forcibly taken from someone, whether it be their clothes, armor, or goods — the natural and cruel fruit of military victory.
H2488.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to take away, to remove, to strip." It describes the action of taking something from someone, hence "what is taken away." The family of this word in Hebrew expresses the idea of withdrawal or deprivation: to strip someone is to take away what covers or protects them.
H2488.emploi: The word "spoil" appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in military and war loot contexts. In Judges 14:19, it refers to the garments of the thirty men that Samson killed, which he offers to those who solved his riddle: the spoil here is the price or reward, taken from the enemy. In 2 Samuel 2:21, Abner encourages Asahel to seize a young fighter and his spoil, meaning to make it his war loot. In both cases, it is the equipment or goods taken from the one defeated: the spoil is the tangible sign of victory.
H2488.portee: This word reminds us that military victory brought not only honor but also material loot: the spoil was the wealth of the victor. For the believer, it illustrates the cost and concrete fruits of battles, and shows that earthly goods were considered legitimate stakes of war. It also invites reflection on what we "strip" from one another, and on the true victory offered by Christ.

sens: a defenseless person facing injustice
a man abandoned to his misery
one who has no earthly help
H2489.detail:
1. The unfortunate is one who finds themselves without protection, exposed to the malice of others. In Psalms 10:8, it is the innocent one whom the wicked watches in ambush, knowing that he cannot defend himself effectively.
2. It is also the man plunged into distress and suffering (Psalms 10:14), one whose condition evokes pity — the orphan perfectly represents this figure: alone, fragile, devoid of the resources that a father or a community would provide.
3. Spiritually, the unfortunate is one who recognizes that he has no earthly help and that only God can intervene for him — it is the portrait of the poor whom the Psalms say the Lord cares for.
H2489.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the idea of what is weak, broken, unable to withstand the storm. The word denotes not moral guilt, but a vulnerability of condition: one who does not have the means for his own defense. It is a term of compassion to describe one who suffers rather than one who acts.
H2489.emploi: The word appears twice in Psalms 10, a psalm that meditates on the tyranny of the wicked and trust in God. First, it designates the innocent victim that the tyrant hunts (v. 8); then, it becomes a call to God: the unfortunate, who has no one to help him, must turn to the Lord (v. 14). It is in this psalm that the word finds its full meaning: not a shameful position, but a call for divine intervention.
H2489.portee: This word reminds the reader that God has a special heart for those who are without resources, without power, without a voice in the system of men. It invites the believer to recognize his own weakness in the face of the injustices of the world and to place his trust in God alone, rather than in his strength or earthly protectors.

sens: Pierce, stab the body with a weapon or a violent blow
Inflict a serious, mortal wound or not
Cause harm, damage
Reach morally, afflict the heart
H2490A.detail:
